raw_text: {"translation": "[11.1.1] [1. On the flesh of the viper.] Not all the fleshes of animals nourish a human being; those of some are even deadly, no less than the drug-like substances which they call deleterious; and of the fleshes that do nourish us some are this alone, nutriments, while some, in addition to nourishing, also possess the power proper to a drug, since by drying or moistening and heating or cooling they alter the body. At any rate, one can clearly see that those of vipers heat and dry when they are dressed, like eels, with oil and salt and dill and leek and, obviously, water in due measure. That they purge the whole body through the skin you may learn also from what I myself experienced while still a young man in our Asia, each instance of which I shall now go through in order. A man sick with the affection called elephas for a while shared the life of his familiars; but when, from association and intercourse with him, some came to share in the affection, and he himself was by now foul-smelling and hideous to look upon, they built a hut for him near the village on a low part of the hill beside a spring and settled the man in it, bringing him food for as many days as sufficed for him to live on. About the rising of the Dog-star a wine, very fragrant, in an earthenware jar was brought to reapers who were reaping near him. The one who brought it set it down near the reapers and went away; and when the time for drinking came for them, their custom was to pour out a krater and mix the wine with water in due measure, but when a young man had taken up the jar and was pouring the wine out into the krater, a dead viper fell out along with it. So the reapers, fearing lest they suffer some harm from the drink, themselves drank water, and as they were departing they bestowed, out of humanity forsooth, the whole of the wine upon the man sick with elephas, judging it better for him to die than to live in such a state. But he, drinking from it, became healthy in a marvellous manner. For the whole mound-like roughness of his skin fell away, like the covering of the soft-shelled animals; and what remained appeared quite soft, like that of crayfish and crabs when the surrounding shell has fallen off. Another such case came about from a similar chance event in Mysia in Asia, not far from our city. A man suffering with elephas set out to make use of naturally hot waters in hope of benefit. He had a concubine, a slave, young and beautiful, who had many lovers; to her the sick man entrusted certain other matters of the household and indeed also the affairs of the storeroom. When they had lodged, while he was using the waters, in a house that had adjoining to it a parched plot full of vipers, one of these fell into a wine-jar lying carelessly about and died in it; the concubine, considering what had chanced to happen a godsend, offered her master his drink from this jar. And he, drinking it, was healed in the same way as the man in the hut. These, then, are now two lessons for you of experience by chance; and a third in addition to them from our own imitation. For when a certain man sick with this disease, more philosophical than the common run, was terribly distressed and kept saying that it was better to die than to live, to him in so wretched a condition I disclosed the two aforementioned chance occurrences. And he—for he was himself experienced in augury and had the use of a friend who excelled marvellously in that study—sat watching the birds together with him and was prompted to imitate what had been learned through experience, and by drinking wine drugged in this way he became leprous. Some time later we cured his lepra too with the customary drugs. A fourth after this man, who had made it his craft to catch live vipers, was in the beginning of that affection, and it was our concern that he be healed as quickly as possible. So having cut a vein of his and purged him with a drug that evacuates black [bile], we advised him to use the vipers he caught, preparing them in a dish, just like eels. This man, then, was treated in this way, the affection dispersing from him by transpiration. Another man, a wealthy one—this man not a countryman of ours, but he came from the middle of Thrace, a dream having urged him to Pergamon—then, the god having ordered him in a dream both to drink of the drug made from vipers every day and to anoint his body externally with it, the affection changed after not many days into lepra, and this disease too was in turn cured by the drugs the god commanded. So the flesh of vipers reaches this degree of drying power; but since some of those who ate it were seized by a most violent thirst, on this account they also call the vipers dipsades. There are those who say, too, that those bitten by them are not filled when they drink, but burst before they cease to be thirsty. For this reason I inquired of those who hunt vipers in Rome, whom they call Marsi, whether they had any sign to teach me distinguishing each of the two kinds of vipers; but they said there was no kind at all of dipsad vipers, but that those living by the sea and in places having much saline soil have salty flesh, and that for this reason many such arise in Libya, while in Italy there are none because of the moistness of the country. These things, then, I heard the Marsi say, yet I cannot state with certainty whether they tell the truth in the whole or also lie in some respect. For that in the places they mentioned some vipers arise having salty flesh seems to me most plausible, since I know that the fleshes of animals change along with their foods; yet I cannot declare that there is no kind of dipsad vipers. The safest course, therefore, is to guard against hunting the vipers in such places for eating or for the preparation of a drug, such as is this famous one which almost all physicians call theriac. And since it is our custom, when we prepare the so-called theriac troches, to remove not only their head but also the tail, I have often reflected that the whole head is perhaps removed reasonably, on account of the venom contained in the mouth, but the tail unreasonably. For one cannot even say this, that it must be done so on account of the residues of the food, both the moist and the dry. For having killed them, and then skinned and opened them up, we take out and throw away all the inner parts, so that only the substance of the flesh is left along with the arteries and veins that grow through it, which have a very small bulk in relation to the whole flesh and are not even visible unless one examines very carefully. The troches, then, which they indeed also call theriac, we prepare as follows. Taking them cleaned, we then boil them in water until they seem to us thoroughly boiled. We throw in dill along with them into the water right from the start, and after the boiling we separate the spines from the flesh, then mix the flesh with bread ground fine. This bread we take not any chance one, but as far as possible the purest and well baked in a klibanos, having salt and leaven in due measure. We dry it beforehand in a dry room free of damp, until it becomes so dry as to be able to be pounded in a mortar. Yet we do not mix it by pounding, but by soaking it in the water in which we boiled the vipers. The flesh itself, before mixing it with the bread, we grind in a cooks' mortar until it becomes thoroughly smooth. And after this, having moulded small thin troches and then dried them in a warm and dry room, we keep them, putting them away again in such a room. These, then, we prepare at the onset of summer, when the flesh of vipers is at its very best. We use them later, pounding and sifting them, then grinding them smooth again and mixing them with the salts prepared for pleasure, and we also put some of them into the theriac. The salts made from roasted vipers are also made at the same season, we throwing the live vipers into a new pot together with the drugs strewn beneath and placed around them, all of which it is not the business of the present treatise to tell now. For perhaps someone will reasonably reproach us also regarding the preparation of the troches, as having gone through it out of season. But since these things have already been said, let them be kept, even if they seem not very properly to belong to the treatise before us. Let what follows be said in the fitting measure. It is fitting to recall the general power of the flesh of vipers, saying that it is strongly drying and dispersing, together with heating moderately. Its power hastens, as it seems, to the skin, moving through it the residues in the body. So a not small multitude of lice is generated in those who have abundant kakochymia in their bodies, and what is called the epidermis separates from the skin and falls away like a scale, in which the thick and earthy of the humours carried to the skin are retained more, by which psorai and leprai and elephantes come about. These things, then, I had to say to you about the fleshes of the viper; next I shall take up the argument again. The fleshes of animals hotter by nature not only nourish us but also heat, those of colder ones cool. In the same way those of drier ones dry, and those of moister ones moisten. Remembering, then, what you learned in the books On Mixtures, when you recognise some animal to be drier in mixture, as for instance the wild boar than the domestic pig, know that its flesh too is more drying, and likewise for the other differences of mixtures, for example that the sheep is drier than the pig, the goat than this, the ox than this, and the lion than this. So too in heat the lion is hotter than the dog, the dog than the bull, the bull than the ox whose testicles have been cut out. In proportion, then, to the superiority in mixture of the other animals their fleshes too will differ. And on this account, wishing to dry the body you will give the flesh of animals drier in mixture, wishing to heat it, that of hotter ones, attempting to make it colder, that of colder ones, and moister, that of moister ones. Not small, too, is the difference of fleshes in some of them having been salted. For they differ altogether, so that often the salted flesh of an animal moistest in mixture is by far more drying than the unsalted flesh of one dry by nature. And roasted flesh is drier than that boiled in water. Some have also written that the fleshes of other animals help both when eaten and when applied on affected parts, for example that of the land hedgehog dried, if drunk, for sufferers from elephantiasis and cachectics and those subject to spasm and nephritics, and further those who have the dropsy called anasarca. If it is by nature able to do these things, its power would be strongly dispersing and drying, like also that of the dried weasel, which indeed benefits epileptics when drunk. The flesh of salted cats, ground smooth and applied, they say draws out splinters, as evidently having a drawing power, and that of mussels suits wounds that have come about from a biting dog. But I find no special power that such wounds require, as do those arising from the bite of a rabid dog. And the flesh of snails, first pounded in a mortar and afterwards ground smooth, becomes most drying of all parts that have excessive moisture, so that it suits even the dropsical. The moisture from them, taken alone by itself without the flesh, is called by most people snail's slime, and mixed with frankincense or aloe or myrrh or some of these or all, until it has the thickness of a cerate, it becomes a glue-holding drug and dries well the suppurating slimy discharges (ὑποπύους μύξους) of the ears. It is also a drying anakollema for fluxes into the eyes, applied on the forehead. Some use it also for splinters, grinding them whole together with their shells, and there are some who use it also for the checking of the menses. The fleshes alone by themselves I too once in the country applied, having ground them smooth, upon a wound that had come about together with a wounding and crushing of a sinew, and the wound was well glued together and the sinew did not become inflamed. He was a hard and rustic man; I did however mix with them, as they were being ground, flour-dust taken from the wall adjoining the mill. Some of the physicians before us have written that myrrh or frankincense must be mixed with them for such use, but I had neither of these outside the city on the farm. One could also mix in smooth roasted (φρικτῆς) resin, if it were at hand. When, however, you wish to take much of the slime of the snails alone, prick their flesh with a stylus. They must not have been caught many days before, for they dry up with time. When fresh they have much of the viscous moisture, which they emit when pricked with the stylus. raw_text: {"translation": "[11.1.2] [2. On soft fat and hard fat.] Soft fat and hard fat. These too are among the most common of the parts in animals. For all well-nourished animals have soft fat or hard fat, whereas the lean and ill-nourished often appear to have none at all, and often so little and so dry that it is difficult to use. Hard fat differs from soft fat in thickness; and hence hard fat arises in animals whose whole nature is more earthy, just as soft fat arises in those whose nature is moister. For this reason, accordingly, soft fat melts easily under fire but, once melted, does not easily congeal; hard fat, on the other hand, neither melts easily, and if it is melted it congeals very quickly and appears much harder than soft fat. A well-nourished pig, then, has the most soft fat, owing to the natural moistness of its mixture, whereas cattle and goats and all the other horned animals, owing to their dryness, produce the most hard fat. But you, if you wish, may call the whole oily and fatty substance in animals hard fat, as most physicians do; and you are also permitted to name this whole genus soft fat. What you are not permitted to do, if you wish not to speak falsely, is to say that the fat of goats is moister than that of pigs. For this latter is nearly the moistest of all the others, and for this reason it is in its activity close to oil in power, though it is more softening than oil and more concocting. And for this reason it is mixed into the poultices suited to inflammations. But for those who suffer biting in the region of the rectum or the colon we inject goat's rather than pig's fat, not because it is more blunting of acridity (for so far as nature is concerned pig's fat blunts more, and for this reason it is mixed also into the drugs that treat ulcers, such as the one called parhygron), but because goat's fat congeals easily on account of its thickness, whereas pig's fat flows away like oil; for this reason we inject the former rather in cases of dysentery and tenesmus, when we wish to soothe their biting. And some, through fineness of particles, blunt acridities more, when the painful agent is in the depth of the bodies that are being bitten. For the coarse-particled passes through whole bodies less, the fine-particled more, and it is mingled with all the biting ichors. In this respect, accordingly, goose fat too blunts more what bites in the depth of bodies. It is also hotter than pig's fat. Between them, indeed, is that of cocks; and that of male animals is always hotter and drier. And among these themselves, that of those whose testicles have been excised is less hot and dry; for the castrated male is always assimilated to the females of the same kind. The common head of the argument, which must be kept in mind, is this: that the differences of the soft fat or hard fat in animals, or however you wish to name this whole genus of the oily and fatty part of the body in animals, always arise according to the mixture of the animals. Since, then, the pig falls short in heat and dryness of nearly all four-footed animals, for this reason it also has soft fat that is less hot and more moist. Now the power of all soft fat is moistening and heating of human bodies; for this must be kept in mind throughout, having been stated at the beginning of this treatise; but the differences among each of them are according to more and less. For the soft fat of the pig, relative to us, possesses moistening abundantly, but heating not in the same way as oil does; rather, the fat of pigs too is at the level of the heat in us. That of bulls is much hotter and drier than that of pigs, we remembering again here too that the male is always drier and hotter than the female, and that the castrated male is assimilated to the female, as indeed is everything young; and that among the young themselves the female is moister and less hot than the male. Thus, then, calf's fat also falls short of that of bulls in heat and dryness, and that of kids of that of goats; and that of she-goats falls short of that of he-goats, and among these again that of bulls of that of lions; for the latter is the most dispersing of nearly all the fats in four-footed animals. For it is also the hottest of them and the most fine-particled, so that if you were to mix it into the drugs suited to ulcers and inflammations, not only will you do no good but you will also do harm, having made the drug more pungent than is fitting. But for chronic hardened swellings and contractures of sinews and, in general, all scirrhous conditions it is most serviceable, cases in which pig's fat appears most ineffective. That of bulls stands roughly equally distant from each: by as much as it is hotter and drier than that of pigs, by so much it falls short of that of lions. Since, then, it is set in the middle, it is reasonably mixed into both kinds of drugs, both those that treat scirrhous conditions and those that concoct inflamed parts, such as the so-called tetrapharmakon, composed of wax and resin and pitch and fat. For into this, whether you put bull's or calf's or he-goat's or she-goat's or pig's fat, you will make a drug that brings to suppuration and concocts. But pig's fat, when put in, is suitable for children and women and, in a word, the soft-fleshed, while that of the bull is useful for diggers and reapers and all who have hard flesh either through natural mixture or through the kind of life they lead. All fat, as it ages, becomes hotter than it was and more fine-particled, and so also more dispersing. This holds for nearly all things that age, those at least that do not first putrefy. For wine and honey and vinegar and cheese and butter and oisypos and every oil, whether mastic oil or castor oil or radish-seed oil or the oil from olives itself, when aged become thinner and more fine-particled, and for this reason appear more pungent to those who taste them and more dispersing to those who use them, in all conditions that are hardening and difficult to dissolve. Now I have said that it appears more pungent to those who taste it. But some of those who corrupt the meanings of words call all such things not pungent but astringent, as far as pepper, as though it made no difference to say astringent or pungent. response.translation: [11.1.2] [2. On soft fat and hard fat.] Soft fat and hard fat. These too are among the most common of the parts in animals. For all well-nourished animals have soft fat or hard fat, whereas the lean and ill-nourished often appear to have none at all, and often so little and so dry that it is difficult to use. Hard fat differs from soft fat in thickness; and hence hard fat arises in animals whose whole nature is more earthy, just as soft fat arises in those whose nature is moister. For this reason, accordingly, soft fat melts easily under fire but, once melted, does not easily congeal; hard fat, on the other hand, neither melts easily, and if it is melted it congeals very quickly and appears much harder than soft fat. A well-nourished pig, then, has the most soft fat, owing to the natural moistness of its mixture, whereas cattle and goats and all the other horned animals, owing to their dryness, produce the most hard fat. But you, if you wish, may call the whole oily and fatty substance in animals hard fat, as most physicians do; and you are also permitted to name this whole genus soft fat. What you are not permitted to do, if you wish not to speak falsely, is to say that the fat of goats is moister than that of pigs. For this latter is nearly the moistest of all the others, and for this reason it is in its activity close to oil in power, though it is more softening than oil and more concocting. And for this reason it is mixed into the poultices suited to inflammations. But for those who suffer biting in the region of the rectum or the colon we inject goat's rather than pig's fat, not because it is more blunting of acridity (for so far as nature is concerned pig's fat blunts more, and for this reason it is mixed also into the drugs that treat ulcers, such as the one called parhygron), but because goat's fat congeals easily on account of its thickness, whereas pig's fat flows away like oil; for this reason we inject the former rather in cases of dysentery and tenesmus, when we wish to soothe their biting. And some, through fineness of particles, blunt acridities more, when the painful agent is in the depth of the bodies that are being bitten. For the coarse-particled passes through whole bodies less, the fine-particled more, and it is mingled with all the biting ichors. In this respect, accordingly, goose fat too blunts more what bites in the depth of bodies. It is also hotter than pig's fat. Between them, indeed, is that of cocks; and that of male animals is always hotter and drier. And among these themselves, that of those whose testicles have been excised is less hot and dry; for the castrated male is always assimilated to the females of the same kind. The common head of the argument, which must be kept in mind, is this: that the differences of the soft fat or hard fat in animals, or however you wish to name this whole genus of the oily and fatty part of the body in animals, always arise according to the mixture of the animals. Since, then, the pig falls short in heat and dryness of nearly all four-footed animals, for this reason it also has soft fat that is less hot and more moist. Now the power of all soft fat is moistening and heating of human bodies; for this must be kept in mind throughout, having been stated at the beginning of this treatise; but the differences among each of them are according to more and less. For the soft fat of the pig, relative to us, possesses moistening abundantly, but heating not in the same way as oil does; rather, the fat of pigs too is at the level of the heat in us. That of bulls is much hotter and drier than that of pigs, we remembering again here too that the male is always drier and hotter than the female, and that the castrated male is assimilated to the female, as indeed is everything young; and that among the young themselves the female is moister and less hot than the male. Thus, then, calf's fat also falls short of that of bulls in heat and dryness, and that of kids of that of goats; and that of she-goats falls short of that of he-goats, and among these again that of bulls of that of lions; for the latter is the most dispersing of nearly all the fats in four-footed animals. For it is also the hottest of them and the most fine-particled, so that if you were to mix it into the drugs suited to ulcers and inflammations, not only will you do no good but you will also do harm, having made the drug more pungent than is fitting. But for chronic hardened swellings and contractures of sinews and, in general, all scirrhous conditions it is most serviceable, cases in which pig's fat appears most ineffective. That of bulls stands roughly equally distant from each: by as much as it is hotter and drier than that of pigs, by so much it falls short of that of lions. Since, then, it is set in the middle, it is reasonably mixed into both kinds of drugs, both those that treat scirrhous conditions and those that concoct inflamed parts, such as the so-called tetrapharmakon, composed of wax and resin and pitch and fat. For into this, whether you put bull's or calf's or he-goat's or she-goat's or pig's fat, you will make a drug that brings to suppuration and concocts. But pig's fat, when put in, is suitable for children and women and, in a word, the soft-fleshed, while that of the bull is useful for diggers and reapers and all who have hard flesh either through natural mixture or through the kind of life they lead. All fat, as it ages, becomes hotter than it was and more fine-particled, and so also more dispersing. This holds for nearly all things that age, those at least that do not first putrefy. raw_text: {"translation": "[11.1.15] [15. On castoreum.] They call the testicles of the beaver castoreum. It is a renowned and much-used drug, so much so that a whole book was written by Archigenes on the use of castoreum. He, then, went through its particular powers; but I, just as with the other drugs, so also with this one shall state its general power, by looking to which one will be able to discover the particular ones for oneself. That it heats is evident. For if you should wish, having worked it perfectly smooth and moistened it with oil, to anoint and rub some part with it, you will clearly perceive that part being heated. Now all heating things, dispersing something of the adjacent substance, immediately also dry it, unless the thing be moist by nature, like oil and water, and take on an acquired hot quality, not a power, just as these very things do when brought near fire and the summer sun. Accordingly castoreum, its consistency being dry and having in addition the heating [property], reasonably dries. This, then, is common to it and to very many other drugs; but it is sufficiently fine-particled, and in this respect it is more powerful than others which heat and dry similarly to it. For fine-particled drugs are more active than coarse-particled ones, even if they have equal power, from their passing through and going into the depth of the bodies with which they come into contact, and especially when these are dense, like the sinewy parts. Clearly, at any rate, such parts are greatly benefited by castoreum for the reason stated. But most physicians are ignorant, in the use of castoreum attending in their minds only to the fact that some part trembles or is convulsed, or is without sensation or without motion, or has impaired sensation or impaired motion, not knowing that such symptoms follow upon dissimilar conditions of the body. But you, having learned from Hippocrates that spasm occurs upon repletion and upon evacuation, where it is necessary to evacuate what is contained contrary to nature in the nerves, both give castoreum to drink and apply it externally upon the skin; but where spasm occurs through excessive dryness, know that this drug is most contrary. By the same reasoning it is also most beneficial to those who tremble because of plethora, but most contrary to those who fall into such an affection through evacuation. Analogously to the affections mentioned I have found also the condition of the hiccuping that arises in the stomach, having made the distinction: if the patients suffer this from plethora, come to the use of castoreum; but if it should arise through dryness and evacuation or through the biting of pungent humours, avoid the drug. One might indeed suspect, attending to its smell and taste, that it has a substance most alien to the human body. In use, however, it appears to do none of the things which such substances do, some harming the stomach, some the belly, some the head, some something else. But this drug, whether you administer it to a moist body needing dryness, or to a cold one [needing] heat, or to a moist and cold one requiring heat and dryness, displays great benefit and inflicts no harm upon any part, and especially when the person is without fever, and, among those with fever, when the fever is not very hot but what one might call a lukewarm fever, such as arises especially in comatose states (kataphorai) and lethargies. To very many we have given castoreum, giving to drink together with white pepper a spoonful of each in honey-water (melikraton), and no one was harmed in any way; rather, when the menses were retained, having first evacuated moderately from the ankle, then giving castoreum with pennyroyal (glechon) or kalaminthe (calamint), I have always found the drug moving a purgation, without the woman being harmed in anything. It also expels retained afterbirths (choria). All these things, then, it does when drunk in honey-water (melikraton). Those whose belly is intractably filled with wind, or who suffer colic or hiccup, in consequence of cold and viscous humours or of thick and flatulent pneuma, it helps when drunk in oxykraton (vinegar-and-water); and whatever it benefits when taken inside the body, these it benefits also when applied upon the skin together with Sicyonian oil or old oil. For the conditions needing more heat it is appropriate also to rub [the part] with it by itself. It helps too if someone, burning it on coals as a fumigation, draws it in through inhalation, and especially the moist and cold affections of the lung and the brain. The lethargic and comatose affections, however, all those with fevers, it is better to treat not by moistening it with any of the oils mentioned, but rather to apply it in rose oil to the head and the neck.", "renderings": [{"target_no": 2, "surface": "καστορίου.]", "english": "castoreum", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 19, "surface": "καστορίου", "english": "castoreum", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 277, "surface": "καστόριον.", "english": "castoreum", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 457, "surface": "καταφοραῖς", "english": "comatose states (kataphorai)", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 476, "surface": "μελικράτου", "english": "honey-water (melikraton)", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 495, "surface": "καλαμίνθης,", "english": "kalaminthe (calamint)", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 542, "surface": "ὀξυκράτου", "english": "oxykraton (vinegar-and-water)", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 607, "surface": "πυρετῶν", "english": "fevers", "uncertain": "n"}], "uncertain_greek": ["ἀρύῃ", "σικυωνίῳ", "δι’ ἑαυτοῦ"]}

raw_text: {"translation": "[11.1.26] [26. On oysters.] The shell of oysters, when burnt, is of a power similar to the shell of the trumpet-shells, and still more fine-particled, or, to put it more safely, less coarse-particled. For all things whose body has an earthy and hard consistency and solidification are considerably coarse-particled, and for this reason it is also fitting to pulverize them carefully. response.translation: [11.1.27] [27. On the cuttlefish.] The shell of the cuttlefish is quite loose-textured, not stony like those of oysters. Now cleansing, as with the other shells of the shell-skinned animals, is common to it along with them, just as drying is too. But the fine-particled quality of its substance belongs to it as something exceptional compared with the others, which is why we also use it, when burnt, for alphoi, ephelis, lentigines and scabies. Moreover, mixed with mined salt it melts away the pterygia that form in the eyes. And even before being burnt, when roasted and finely ground, it both brightens the teeth and dries wounds. On account of the moderate degree of its roughness we are also accustomed to use it for the great roughnesses in the eyes which they call sycoses, carving out of it something resembling a collyrium in shape and rubbing them with it so as to draw blood. For when this has been done, the reducing collyria too act better upon them.

response.translation: [11.1.29] [29. On oesypum-bearing wool.] Wool that is still dirty, and for this reason called by some "oesypum-bearing", usefully receives the affusions applied to parts that have been bruised or struck in any way whatever, contributing to the benefit derived from them by means of the oesypum. response.translation: [11.1.33] [33. On snails.] Snails, whole, burnt together with their shells, with omphakitis gall-nut and white pepper mixed in with them, are of great benefit in dysenteries in which the ulcers are not yet putrid. The proportion should be one part of the pepper, two of the gall-nut, and four of the ash of the snails. Having made these thoroughly smooth, sprinkle them on the foods and give them to drink in water or in wine that is white and harsh. Without being mixed with gall-nut, the ash of snails is of a sufficiently drying power, which also has, on account of the burning, something of heat. He himself, however, recommends that after the use of that blood one sprinkle on either chalcanthon or hemlock seed; and he says that when this is done the hairs either do not grow at all or grow downy, as if he were bringing in the seed of hemlock as some trifling drug, and not one sufficient by itself to cool vigorously whatever parts it is applied to. As food, however, many often use blood, that of the hare and of hens and of goats; but that of the hare and of hens not a few even of those in the cities, while that of goats those in the countryside, filling the goats' stomachs with it together with the fat, as Homer said the suitors did. Some things, as has also been said before, are at once both foods and drugs; of these [we treat] in this treatise insofar as they are drugs, not insofar as they are foods. For indeed those who have given the blood of the goat with honey to those suffering from dropsy administer it as a drug, not as a food, as do those who have used it roasted against dysentery or against a flux of the belly. And it seems to me that someone came to this use having supposed that its coarse-particled and earthy quality together with heat is drying. For hemorrhages of the meninges, finding the blood of cock and hen written up by them, I neither hoped that it would do anything great, and I was, on the one hand, ashamed to judge it by experience, lest I should seem meddlesome or foolish if, passing over so many and such approved drugs, I hoped that the blood of these birds would accomplish more; and on the other hand, since such a hemorrhage is perilous, it did not seem to me right to resort to any of the untried things. This too is false, just as is the claim that hair does not grow in the armpits, which Xenocrates, doing well, discredited as untrue. He himself, however, recommends that after the use of that blood one sprinkle on either chalcanthon or hemlock seed; and he says that when this is done the hairs either do not grow at all or grow downy, as if he were bringing in the seed of hemlock as some trifling drug, and not one sufficient by itself to cool vigorously whatever parts it is applied to. Some also smear the blood of the bat on the genitals of boys, thinking that by this they will keep the parts without pubic hair for a very long time. And yet they ought to have thought not 'for a very long time', but that they would remain such for ever, just as they suppose about the armpits too. Now from the part being strongly cooled it is reasonable that something of this kind should come about; but the blood of the bat is not cold in power to so great a degree, for no blood at all is cold. As food, however, many often use blood, that of the hare and of hens and of goats; but that of the hare and of hens not a few even of those in the cities, while that of goats those in the countryside, filling the goats' stomachs with it together with the fat, as Homer said the suitors did. But our discourse now is not about things taken in the role of food, but about those taken as drugs. Some things, as has also been said before, are at once both foods and drugs; of these [we treat] in this treatise insofar as they are drugs, not insofar as they are foods. For indeed those who have given the blood of the goat with honey to those suffering from dropsy administer it as a drug, not as a food, as do those who have used it roasted against dysentery or against a flux of the belly. And it seems to me that someone came to this use having supposed that its coarse-particled and earthy quality together with heat is drying. For hemorrhages of the meninges, finding the blood of cock and hen written up by them, I neither hoped that it would do anything great, and I was, on the one hand, ashamed to judge it by experience, lest I should seem meddlesome or foolish if, passing over so many and such approved drugs, I hoped that the blood of these birds would accomplish more; and on the other hand, since such a hemorrhage is perilous, it did not seem to me right to resort to any of the untried things. For such an experiment is thus dangerous, and is reasonably undertaken only by kings upon wicked men. I condemned in advance also the blood of lambs, which some say cures epilepsy when drunk; so I was not going to judge this by experience either. But if anyone wishes to make the test, I know clearly that the very writers of such things will be condemned. For all drugs which, when drunk, benefit epileptics are of the cutting power, and the blood of lambs is least of all of such a kind. As for what is said by Xenocrates about the blood of kids, thinking it possible that it might accomplish something because of the admixture of vinegar, I referred it to one of those living in the countryside to carry out, a man fond of farming but educated in the primary education; and he says that, having used it on two who spat blood, he found some benefit. But it seemed to me, from what he related, that neither of them had spat it either from an artery or from the larynx or the lung. Xenocrates, at any rate, writes in the first book On the Benefit from Animals, where he discusses kids, word for word as follows: 'Very useful for those who spit blood. One must, while it has not yet congealed, mix with about half a kotyle an equal amount of pungent vinegar, then, having boiled it up, divide it into three and give one part to be gulped down each day.' So it is possible for you, at some time in the countryside, when you lack the other things, to use this too, since the trial is without danger. The blood of the bear, applied hot to abscesses, may possibly ripen them. I shall add to the account also that of the goat and of the he-goat and of the bull. And it is open to you, if you wish, passing over countless of the readily available drugs by which we ripen abscesses, to slaughter bears and bulls and he-goats, evidently at each use. For certainly no one who has applied it once to the affected part will demand what the drug promises, nor indeed when it has already become cold so as to have congealed.

raw_text: {"translation": "[10.2.7] [7. On milk.] Milk. This has a twofold use, the one as nourishment, the other as a drug. Now the healthiest milk, just like blood, is pure and unmixed, partaking neither of bitterness nor of acidity nor of pungency nor of saltiness nor of foul smell, but, as one might say, fragrant or odourless, or, if anything, partaking of some slight fragrance. It is evident that it is also pleasant when tasted, having a slight sweetness, just like healthy blood, from which also the generation of milk takes place. Such milk is most advantageous against pungent and biting fluxes, not only washing them away from the troubled parts—for this it has in common with water—but also plastering itself around the bodies, so that what flows in does not fall upon them bare. And not only in this does it have the advantage over water, but also in its washing them round, because it contains in itself a cleansing moisture, the one called whey, which is first washed away and in addition washes the bodies. With all the rest, which is thick and oily, it plasters itself around them in the very manner in which fat and suet do, and the white of an egg, and the cerate made from washed wax and oil; for these too soothe the bitings from pungent ichors, by being plastered around the bodies, having a non-biting nature. raw_text: {"translation": "[10.2.8] [8. On whey of milk.] Whey, as has been said, has a cleansing power, and it is taken for the purpose of evacuating the bowel and is injected by means of clysters, cleansing round about and washing away without biting the pungencies in the intestines. And one would do best to wash out ulcers that contain pungent ichors with whey instead of water. And as for the drugs that are dispersing of ecchymoses and black discolorations, these too it is better to wash round with whey, not with water. In this way, then, we use it also for bruises beneath the eyes and for hyposphagmata, mixing it with the drugs proper to these conditions. The cheesy and thick part of the milk is rather plastered on, and in this respect it blunts the pungencies. But when it takes on in addition some other drying power, it becomes an excellent drug for dysenterics and for all the pungent fluxes in the bowel; and it takes this on by means of red-hot stones, previously heated through, that are thrown into it. These must be the ones they call pebbles (kachlekes), and the milk must be boiled until the greater part of the whey-like moisture in it has been used up. We, however, produce the same or even a better power by means of red-hot iron cylinders thrown into it. For iron, as has been said, partakes of an astringent power, and for this reason I myself had several cylinders prepared, attached to the ends of spits, so that one may easily lift the iron by the handle once it has been heated. And just as with cauteries, so too I wrap the handles of these in rags. Whole milk is useful against the pungent fluxes of the eyes, both by itself and together with the simple collyria, and further against hyposphagmata and bruises beneath the eyes; and indeed, applied on the outside upon the eyelids, together with rose-oil and egg, when those suffering from ophthalmia are about to sleep, it ripens their inflammations; but let this milk be a woman's, fresh, dripped from the breasts. We inject it also into ulcerated wombs, both by itself and also mixing it with the drugs that treat without biting, with which it is mixed, and whenever we soothe the ulcers in the seat that are painful because of pungent ichors or inflammations or folds that have risen up. In this way too we use it for the affections of the genitals and, simply, for all that need soothing because of inflammation or biting or malignancy. For this reason, then, it is also applied to cancerous ulcers, mixed with anodyne drugs, such as especially those made with pompholyx. And milk was said to have in itself also a certain fatty and, as it were, oil-like nature, and I said that this is present in greatest quantity in cow's milk, and that when it has been parted from the rest of the milk, this oily part, having come to be by itself, is called butter, whereas when it has set together with the whole milk—the whey-like moisture obviously having been separated off in the setting—it makes the cheese oily. And some of the cow's-milk cheeses become so oily that something oil-like flows out of them. With time, both these and all the others will appear more pungent to you when you taste and smell them. And once, when a cow's-milk cheese had been brought to me, judging from its smell that it was pungent, I threw it aside; and I for my part supposed it had been used up by the household servants, but the one accustomed to keep such things, after a long time, bringing it out from the storeroom, asked what indeed I ordered concerning it. raw_text: {"translation": "[10.2.13] [13. On bile.] This humour has been demonstrated to be the hottest of the humours in each animal. Just as, then, animals have blood and flesh of unlike mixture, so by the same reasoning they have bile too. For in the hottest animals the bile too must necessarily exceed the biles of the other animals, while in those less hot than these this humour too must fall short proportionately, by as much as it falls short in the others as well. For you have learned that the humours in each of the blooded animals are in all four: blood, phlegm, and bile both yellow and black. You have also learned that it is the custom not only of physicians but of all Greeks to name yellow bile simply 'bile', on the assumption that those who hear it will supply the name of the colour, but not to name black bile simply 'bile', but with the addition of this whole phrase, 'black bile'. But you also know that they sometimes call yellow bile 'pale yellow', and that in the bladder upon the liver we sometimes see it pale yellow and sometimes yellow in the dissections of animals. You have heard too that the yellow is hotter than the pale yellow by just as much as it is also thicker. For when a serous moisture is mixed with yellow bile the result is that the pale yellow comes about, just as, conversely, the pale yellow, when heated further, is rendered thick in consistency and yellow in colour. And so indeed among animals too it appears yellow in the hotter ones and pale yellow in the less hot. And when the hot animals happen to have gone hungry and thirsty, it turns toward a black colour, having this sometimes verdigris-like, sometimes dark blue, and sometimes the colour of woad, which is duskier than that of cabbage. So you too must attend to the colour of the biles when you prepare a drug in which some bile is also contained. They mix the bile of the bull into the so-called cycliscs and trochiscs, such as that of Andron and of Polyeides and of Pasion and the one of Bitinus. But when they prepare any of the drugs useful for the eyes, [they use that] of hyena and cock and partridge and certain other animals. The bull's bile is obviously hotter and more drying than that of castrated oxen. For the castrated animal is always assimilated to the female and the young. Just as, then, these exceed the mature in moisture but fall short in heat, in the same way the castrated ox falls short of bulls. And in certain bulls I have seen the bile dark blue, the yellow having been over-roasted; this I did not think fit to throw into the drug being prepared, but chose the moderately yellow bile of another bull. For that bull had been excessively distressed, being dragged with violent bonds, so that it is quite clear that, having also become enraged in this struggle, it had acquired a hotter mixture. It is likely too that it was both thirsty and hungry while being violently hauled along. To put it in sum: just as urine appears moderately pale yellow on moderate drinking, but yellow in those who have been thirsty and have abstained from food and have laboured much, and white in those who have been filled and made drunk, so too bile changes its colours, toward the yellower in exercises and fasting and thirst, and toward the whiter in the opposite conditions. Know, then, that if you put into the drug being prepared a bile that is sufficiently yellow, you will make it hotter; if a pale yellow one, moderately hot; and if one that is slack and watery, falling short of the appropriate mixture by as much as the bile too has turned toward the whiter. So too, then, for those who open closed haemorrhoids by means of bull's bile, it has appeared sometimes weak and sometimes pungent beyond what is appropriate. Now some difference arises also from the body that is being treated with the bile, which may be of acute or dull sensation, and readily or hardly affected. But from the bile itself, as I said, the variation is no small one. At any rate the same man is bitten more by yellow bile and less by pale yellow. It is quite clear, then, even from its opening the haemorrhoids, how pungent this humour is; but it also appears biting to those who use it themselves, and for this reason we are wary of using yellow bile alone by itself for any other disease or symptom. For indeed the aforementioned cycliscs take only a little of the bile, and the drugs compounded for sharpness of sight, which take some of them hyena's bile, others that of partridge or cock or some other animal, have honey mixed in, and juice of fennel or opobalsam. The bile of some animals has been especially praised among physicians as both sharpening the sight and at the same time dispersing the beginnings of cataracts, as that of the fish—they call it callionymus—and of the hyena and the sea scorpion and the hen and the partridge. The weakest is that of pigs, to such a degree that it is not unbearable even to ulcers; indeed it appears the most watery of all biles, except for that of wild pigs that live in the mountains. For just as the whole flesh of these is hotter and drier, so too is the bile. Some use the bile of domestic pigs for ulcers in the ears, not a disreputable drug, and you too may use it when none of the compound drugs is at hand, for there are countless of them. According to the magnitude of the condition some other bile of another animal might also be fitting. For when the ulcer is both chronic and contains much ichor and pus, it will tolerate even the more drying biles, such as that of sheep, slightly more pungent than that of pigs, and more than this that of goats, to which that of bears and of oxen is somewhat similar. That of bulls is stronger than these, but falls short of that of hyenas. And this in turn is itself [compared] to that of the callionymus and the sea scorpion and the sea tortoise. Some have written that the bile of the wild goat helps those suffering from night-blindness. The biles of all the winged animals too are more pungent and more drying than those in the quadrupeds, and among the winged ones themselves those of hens and partridges are the better for medical use. Those of hawks and eagles are sufficiently pungent, and are also corrosive, for which reason they also appear verdigris-like in colour, and sometimes even black. Knowing, then, these differences among them, and knowing also which of the affections need to be dried more and which less, if you have tested any one bile whatsoever by its works, you will be able from those to pass over to the others by method, so as always to take up the one fitting the affection. For since the intensity belonging to each power lies in the realm of conjecture, you must pass from some determinate starting-point to the untested material, having learned from what has been tested before the degrees of superiority among them. raw_text: {"translation": "[10.2.14] [14. On sweat.] Sweat. This too is one of the fluids generated in the body of the animal, having the same matter and the same mode of generation as urine. For the generation of both is from the liquid that is drunk, when it is heated in the body and at the same time takes on something of a bilious substance. But sweat has been worked up to a greater degree, having passed through all the intervening parts as far as the skin. Sweats and urines must, however, necessarily differ from one another in accordance with the mixtures of the animals, which vary from one another both by nature and according to age, and not a little also according to the preceding regimen. It is clear too, even if it is sometimes left unmentioned, that what pertains to the seasons of the year and the present condition of the weather, and further the regions, produces no small difference in the bodies of animals. But for the sake of brevity in the account I am accustomed to embrace all such things under one heading, saying that they vary in accordance with the mixture of the air that surrounds us. For this embraces the differences among regions in respect of heat and cold, just as it does the seasons of the year and the present or the preceding condition. So whenever the discussion is about urines or sweats or blood or fat or suet or any other of the things in the body, when we distinguish the differences among animals, one must understand the discussion as referring to healthy bodies that have the mean condition of their own proper mixture. So too with sweat: that it partakes of the quality called salty and briny, taste bears witness. For sweat, often flowing into the mouth against our will, displays the said quality, and often it also shows along with it a clear bitterness. Its colour too reveals its nature. For just as urine according to nature is moderately pale yellow, so too is sweat. You will readily recognize this in those who bathe, when they are scraped with the strigil without oil. For it collects in the hollow of the strigil, displaying both the colour such as I have described and the taste, having the salty clearly, but the bitter faintly. But about urine the physicians have written even more than is fitting, because it is collected abundantly every day by all men, privately and publicly. About sweats, however, either nothing, or rather some of those over-curious things that border on sorcery. And apart from such things, some have recorded superfluous things that can be accomplished by other medical material. In the wrestling-schools the sweat of those exercising is mixed with the floor-dust (πάτος) — some of those who affect Attic diction over-curiously call it κονίσαλος — and it contributes something to the bare floor-dust toward the dispersing of swellings contrary to nature. If henna-oil is not available, it suffices to mix in good rose-oil. This drug is also quite useful for women who after childbirth choose to quench their milk, when it has, so to speak, curdled in the breasts. Starting from it you can also use it for other similar affections. I myself, at any rate, once used it on a bubo and saw the swelling quickly subside.

raw_text: {"translation": "[10.2.27] [27. On the dung of geese and storks.] The dung of geese is useless because of its great pungency; and I reckon that of hawks and eagles is also. But the difficulty of procuring all such material is in itself something to be avoided. Taking their start precisely from this, some people testify all the more to strong powers in materials of this kind, since they will not easily be refuted, like those who have written that the dung of storks cures epileptics. But this, although it happens to be far easier to procure than many of the other things they write about, is nevertheless superfluous, in addition to the fact that what has been written about it is not even true. At any rate, someone who was persuaded by those who write such things and drank some of this dung gained no benefit. Indeed, even before trial, those who write these things reveal the worthlessness of what they promise. For since people have difficulty in breathing in many ways, they add in their account neither what suits all of them nor what suits these particular ones or this one. Some, to be sure, of those who have written say that such things are remedies not for difficulty of breathing simply, but for orthopnoea—stork's dung and owl's blood and human urine and other things more absurd than these—not knowing that a phlegmatic and viscous humour blocking the bronchia of the lung becomes the cause of this affection, and that the cure lies in evacuating it, and that its evacuation comes about with its being coughed up along with a cough, and that this cannot happen unless a rather pungent drug has been drunk many times. But these people are so full of nonsense, or are charlatans, or I know not what to call them, that they say that each of these absurd drinks, once drunk, frees the sufferers from their difficulty of breathing—a thing which, not even if someone were able to insert a probe into the lung and through it remove the humour plastered on, would have been accomplished at a single attempt. response.translation: [10.2.27] [27. On the dung of geese and storks.] The dung of geese is useless because of its great pungency; and I reckon that of hawks and eagles is also. But the difficulty of procuring all such material is in itself something to be avoided. Taking their start precisely from this, some people testify all the more to strong powers in materials of this kind, since they will not easily be refuted, like those who have written that the dung of storks cures epileptics. But this, although it happens to be far easier to procure than many of the other things they write about, is nevertheless superfluous, in addition to the fact that what has been written about it is not even true. At any rate, someone who was persuaded by those who write such things and drank some of this dung gained no benefit. Indeed, even before trial, those who write these things reveal the worthlessness of what they promise. For since people have difficulty in breathing in many ways, they add in their account neither what suits all of them nor what suits these particular ones or this one. Some, to be sure, of those who have written say that such things are remedies not for difficulty of breathing simply, but for orthopnoea—stork's dung and owl's blood and human urine and other things more absurd than these—not knowing that a phlegmatic and viscous humour blocking the bronchia of the lung becomes the cause of this affection, and that the cure lies in evacuating it, and that its evacuation comes about with its being coughed up along with a cough, and that this cannot happen unless a rather pungent drug has been drunk many times. But these people are so full of nonsense, or are charlatans, or I know not what to call them, that they say that each of these absurd drinks, once drunk, frees the sufferers from their difficulty of breathing—a thing which, not even if someone were able to insert a probe into the lung and through it remove the humour plastered on, would have been accomplished at a single attempt. It would therefore have been better for them to say not that this particular blood or urine cures difficulty of breathing if it be drunk [once], but if it be drunk [habitually]; and better still, that it will not cure wholly and in every case, not even if it be drunk continuously, but that it has cured many, and many it has benefited, yet without completely freeing them from the disease. But let us now leave these people and go on to the continuation of the argument. For since every dung has the pungent and dispersing quality, it is according to the more and the less in one's having this power than another that the particular differences among them arise, and for this reason some treat this particular affection more, others that one.

raw_text: {"translation": "[9.1.2] [2. On the differences of the earth that is customarily so named.] I said that all Greeks customarily give the name \"earth\" to that which, when it is thrown into liquid, is at once dissolved and becomes mud. Of this, then, one kind is that which men cultivate, having certain differences in its own right (κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον λόγον), in being oily and viscous—a kind which is in every case also black in colour—while the other is more crumbly and non-oily, which they call argil, this too being in some degree whiter. These differences are the most opposed; the others lie between these, either approaching more nearly to the one or to the other, and some seem to be exactly in the middle, standing at an equal distance from both. There are also differences of earth that arise from admixture of bodies of a different kind, insofar as they are stony and sandy; and they separate the mixed-in substance from such earths by soaking and kneading them with much water, until they make the whole liquid. For when this settles, all the stony and sandy matter carried in it sinks to the bottom, while the exact earth floats above. For something of this sort happens also in the case of the Lemnian earth, which some call Lemnian miltos and certain others Lemnian seal, because of the seal sacred to Artemis which is impressed upon it. For the priestess, taking this earth with a certain local honour—not with animals being sacrificed, but with wheat and barley given in return to the place—conveys it to the city, and having kneaded it with water and made a liquid mud and stirred this violently, then having let it settle, she first removes the water on the surface, then, taking the oily part of the earth beneath it and leaving behind only the stony and sandy matter that has settled, which is indeed useless, she dries the oily mud to such a degree until it comes to the consistency of soft wax, and taking small portions of this she impresses upon them the sacred seal of Artemis, and then again dries them in the shade until it is rendered exactly free of moisture, and this becomes the drug known to all physicians, the Lemnian seal. For so some name it, as I said, because of the seal impressed upon it, just as some also, because of its colour, call it Lemnian miltos. It has, then, the same colour as miltos, but differs from it in not staining when it is touched, as that one does, and also in respect of the hill in Lemnos, which is wholly tawny in colour, on which there is neither tree nor rock nor plant, but only earth of this sort. Three differences of it are found: one, the aforesaid, of the sacred earth, which no one else touches except the priestess; a second, different one, of the true miltos, which the carpenters especially use; and a third, of the cleansing (ῥυπούσης) kind, which those of the washers of linens and garments who so wish use. Having read in Dioscorides and certain others that goat's blood is mixed with the Lemnian earth, and that from the mud produced by this mixture the priestess moulds and seals what they call Lemnian seals, I desired myself to investigate the proportion of the mixture. Just as, then, I travelled to Cyprus for the sake of the mines in it, and to Coele Syria, which is a part of Palestine, for the sake of asphalt and certain other things in it worth investigating, so too I did not hesitate to sail to Lemnos, intending to see how much of the blood is mixed with the earth. And on the second occasion of coming from Asia to Rome, travelling on foot through Thrace and Macedonia, I sailed first from Alexandria Troas to Lemnos, having found a ship putting out for Thessalonica, the ship-master having agreed to put in first at Lemnos; and he did put in, but not at the city where he should have. For at the start I did not even know that there were two cities on the island, but supposed that, like Samos and Chios and Cos and Andros and Tenos and all the islands in the Aegean, so too Lemnos had a single city bearing the same name as the whole island. But when I disembarked from the ship, I learned that the city was called Myrina, and that the hill was neither in connection with Philoctetes nor in connection with the temple of Hephaestus in the territory of that city, but in the other, called Hephaestias, and that that city was not even near Myrina; and since the ship-master could not wait for me, I deferred to a later time, when I should come from Rome to Asia, the viewing of Hephaestias. And this was accomplished for me, just as I hoped and proposed. For when, having crossed from Italy to Macedonia and having travelled through almost the whole of it, I arrived at Philippi, which is a city bordering on Thrace, going down from there to the nearby sea, which is a hundred and twenty stades distant, I sailed first to Thasos, somewhere near two hundred stades, from there to Lemnos seven hundred, then again from Lemnos the same seven hundred to Alexandria Troas. And for this reason I have deliberately written about the voyage and the stades, so that if anyone wishes to see Hephaestias himself just as I did, knowing its position, he may thus prepare for the voyage. For in the whole island of Lemnos, Hephaestias lies in the part toward the east and Myrina in the part toward the west. And what is said by the poet about Hephaestus, \"he fell in Lemnos,\" seems to me to have set up (ἐπίστασθαι) the myth because of the nature of the hill. For it appears most like something burnt, both in colour and because nothing grows on it. To this hill, then, the priestess came, at the time when I set foot on the island, and casting a certain number of grains of wheat and barley onto the earth and performing certain other acts in accordance with the local reverence, she filled a whole wagon with the earth. And having conveyed it to the city, as I said just now, she prepared the much-talked-of Lemnian seals. It seemed good to me, then, to inquire whether they had ever before received in their tradition any account of goat's or she-goat's blood being mixed with this earth. At this inquiry all who heard laughed, being not ordinary men but very well educated both in other matters and in the whole local history. But I also received a book from one of them, written earlier by one of the local men, in which he taught the whole use of the Lemnian earth, whence I too did not hesitate to make trial of the drug, taking twenty thousand seals. And the man himself who gave the book, being counted among the first men of Hephaestias, used the drug for many purposes. For both on wounds, old ones and those hard to cicatrize, and on viper-bites and in general bites of venomous animals, and in cases of deadly drugs, giving it not only beforehand but also afterwards, he used the seal. He said also that he had experience of the drug made with juniper berries, into which Lemnian earth also is put, which provokes vomiting, if someone drinks the protective remedy while the deadly drug is still in the belly. But of this we too have experience in the case of the sea-hare and cantharides, when people suspected that they had taken something of this sort, and immediately vomited everything upon the drug made with the Lemnian seal, and afterwards suffered none of the symptoms that follow sea-hare and cantharides, even though the administration of the deadly drugs was proved. But whether against the other deadly drugs, those called deleterious, the drug made with juniper berries and Lemnian earth has the same power, is unclear to me. The man from Hephaestias went so far as to declare that it even cures the bite of a mad dog, when drunk in diluted wine and applied to the ulcer in very pungent vinegar. But with vinegar he said it cures also the bites of the other venomous creatures, with leaves of herbs applied externally, which we have learned to be opposed to putrefactions. He praised most of all scordium, then the slender centaury, then horehound. On malignant and putrefactive ulcers at any rate, whenever I used the Lemnian earth, it helped greatly. The use is in accordance with the magnitude of the badness of the ulcer. For the foul-smelling and very flabby and dirty ulcer admits the Lemnian earth dissolved in very pungent vinegar to a muddy consistency, in the same way as the troches, of which different people use different ones—I mean those of Polyeides and Pasion and Andron, and this one now mentioned, called Betinos. For all these, drying strongly, benefit the malignant ulcers, being diluted sometimes with sweet wine, sometimes with boiled-down must, sometimes with honeyed wine, sometimes with some of the white wines or the tawny or the yellow, as the need may command. For these matters will be distinguished elsewhere. Likewise they are also sometimes diluted with vinegar, and with wine or water or oxymel, or with vinegar-and-water and honey-and-water. And the Lemnian earth, diluted with each of the things mentioned, is a suitable drug both for the agglutination of fresh wounds and for the cure of chronic or hard-to-cicatrize or malignant ulcers. And likewise all the other medicinal earth. For it will be necessary to distinguish, just as earlier we distinguished from the elemental earth—in which stones too were included—the earth that is dissolved into mud, so now from the cultivated earth the medicinal. For it is no worse to name thus that which we use for treatments, although even of the cultivated earth the oily kind is useful for the treatment of all parts that need to be dried; whence in Alexandria and Egypt many use it by their own choice, many as a result of dreams. response.translation: [9.1.2] [2. On the differences of the earth that is customarily so named.] I said that all Greeks customarily give the name "earth" to that which, when it is thrown into liquid, is at once dissolved and becomes mud. Of this, then, one kind is that which men cultivate, having certain differences in its own right (κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον λόγον), in being oily and viscous—a kind which is in every case also black in colour—while the other is more crumbly and non-oily, which they call argil, this too being in some degree whiter. These differences are the most opposed; the others lie between these, either approaching more nearly to the one or to the other, and some seem to be exactly in the middle, standing at an equal distance from both. There are also differences of earth that arise from admixture of bodies of a different kind, insofar as they are stony and sandy; and they separate the mixed-in substance from such earths by soaking and kneading them with much water, until they make the whole liquid. For when this settles, all the stony and sandy matter carried in it sinks to the bottom, while the exact earth floats above. For something of this sort happens also in the case of the Lemnian earth, which some call Lemnian miltos and certain others Lemnian seal, because of the seal sacred to Artemis which is impressed upon it. For the priestess, taking this earth with a certain local honour—not with animals being sacrificed, but with wheat and barley given in return to the place—conveys it to the city, and having kneaded it with water and made a liquid mud and stirred this violently, then having let it settle, she first removes the water on the surface, then, taking the oily part of the earth beneath it and leaving behind only the stony and sandy matter that has settled, which is indeed useless, she dries the oily mud to such a degree until it comes to the consistency of soft wax, and taking small portions of this she impresses upon them the sacred seal of Artemis, and then again dries them in the shade until it is rendered exactly free of moisture, and this becomes the drug known to all physicians, the Lemnian seal. For so some name it, as I said, because of the seal impressed upon it, just as some also, because of its colour, call it Lemnian miltos. It has, then, the same colour as miltos, but differs from it in not staining when it is touched, as that one does, and also in respect of the hill in Lemnos, which is wholly tawny in colour, on which there is neither tree nor rock nor plant, but only earth of this sort. Three differences of it are found: one, the aforesaid, of the sacred earth, which no one else touches except the priestess; a second, different one, of the true miltos, which the carpenters especially use; and a third, of the cleansing (ῥυπούσης) kind, which those of the washers of linens and garments who so wish use. Having read in Dioscorides and certain others that goat's blood is mixed with the Lemnian earth, and that from the mud produced by this mixture the priestess moulds and seals what they call Lemnian seals, I desired myself to investigate the proportion of the mixture. Just as, then, I travelled to Cyprus for the sake of the mines in it, and to Coele Syria, which is a part of Palestine, for the sake of asphalt and certain other things in it worth investigating, so too I did not hesitate to sail to Lemnos, intending to see how much of the blood is mixed with the earth. And on the second occasion of coming from Asia to Rome, travelling on foot through Thrace and Macedonia, I sailed first from Alexandria Troas to Lemnos, having found a ship putting out for Thessalonica, the ship-master having agreed to put in first at Lemnos; and he did put in, but not at the city where he should have. For at the start I did not even know that there were two cities on the island, but supposed that, like Samos and Chios and Cos and Andros and Tenos and all the islands in the Aegean, so too Lemnos had a single city bearing the same name as the whole island. But when I disembarked from the ship, I learned that the city was called Myrina, and that the hill was neither in connection with Philoctetes nor in connection with the temple of Hephaestus in the territory of that city, but in the other, called Hephaestias, and that that city was not even near Myrina; and since the ship-master could not wait for me, I deferred to a later time, when I should come from Rome to Asia, the viewing of Hephaestias. And this was accomplished for me, just as I hoped and proposed. For when, having crossed from Italy to Macedonia and having travelled through almost the whole of it, I arrived at Philippi, which is a city bordering on Thrace, going down from there to the nearby sea, which is a hundred and twenty stades distant, I sailed first to Thasos, somewhere near two hundred stades, from there to Lemnos seven hundred, then again from Lemnos the same seven hundred to Alexandria Troas. And for this reason I have deliberately written about the voyage and the stades, so that if anyone wishes to see Hephaestias himself just as I did, knowing its position, he may thus prepare for the voyage. For in the whole island of Lemnos, Hephaestias lies in the part toward the east and Myrina in the part toward the west. And what is said by the poet about Hephaestus, "he fell in Lemnos," seems to me to have set up (ἐπίστασθαι) the myth because of the nature of the hill. For it appears most like something burnt, both in colour and because nothing grows on it. To this hill, then, the priestess came, at the time when I set foot on the island, and casting a certain number of grains of wheat and barley onto the earth and performing certain other acts in accordance with the local reverence, she filled a whole wagon with the earth. And having conveyed it to the city, as I said just now, she prepared the much-talked-of Lemnian seals. It seemed good to me, then, to inquire whether they had ever before received in their tradition any account of goat's or she-goat's blood being mixed with this earth. At this inquiry all who heard laughed, being not ordinary men but very well educated both in other matters and in the whole local history. But I also received a book from one of them, written earlier by one of the local men, in which he taught the whole use of the Lemnian earth, whence I too did not hesitate to make trial of the drug, taking twenty thousand seals. And the man himself who gave the book, being counted among the first men of Hephaestias, used the drug for many purposes. For both on wounds, old ones and those hard to cicatrize, and on viper-bites and in general bites of venomous animals, and in cases of deadly drugs, giving it not only beforehand but also afterwards, he used the seal. He said also that he had experience of the drug made with juniper berries, into which Lemnian earth also is put, which provokes vomiting, if someone drinks the protective remedy while the deadly drug is still in the belly. But of this we too have experience in the case of the sea-hare and cantharides, when people suspected that they had taken something of this sort, and immediately vomited everything upon the drug made with the Lemnian seal, and afterwards suffered none of the symptoms that follow sea-hare and cantharides, even though the administration of the deadly drugs was proved. But whether against the other deadly drugs, those called deleterious, the drug made with juniper berries and Lemnian earth has the same power, is unclear to me. The man from Hephaestias went so far as to declare that it even cures the bite of a mad dog, when drunk in diluted wine and applied to the ulcer in very pungent vinegar. But with vinegar he said it cures also the bites of the other venomous creatures, with leaves of herbs applied externally, which we have learned to be opposed to putrefactions. He praised most of all scordium, then the slender centaury, then horehound. On malignant and putrefactive ulcers at any rate, whenever I used the Lemnian earth, it helped greatly. The use is in accordance with the magnitude of the badness of the ulcer. For the foul-smelling and very flabby and dirty ulcer admits the Lemnian earth dissolved in very pungent vinegar to a muddy consistency, in the same way as the troches, of which different people use different ones—I mean those of Polyeides and Pasion and Andron, and this one now mentioned, called Betinos. For all these, drying strongly, benefit the malignant ulcers, being diluted sometimes with sweet wine, sometimes with boiled-down must, sometimes with honeyed wine, sometimes with some of the white wines or the tawny or the yellow, as the need may command. For these matters will be distinguished elsewhere. Likewise they are also sometimes diluted with vinegar, and with wine or water or oxymel, or with vinegar-and-water and honey-and-water. And the Lemnian earth, diluted with each of the things mentioned, is a suitable drug both for the agglutination of fresh wounds and for the cure of chronic or hard-to-cicatrize or malignant ulcers. And likewise all the other medicinal earth. For it will be necessary to distinguish, just as earlier we distinguished from the elemental earth—in which stones too were included—the earth that is dissolved into mud, so now from the cultivated earth the medicinal. For it is no worse to name thus that which we use for treatments, although even of the cultivated earth the oily kind is useful for the treatment of all parts that need to be dried; whence in Alexandria and Egypt many use it by their own choice, many as a result of dreams. At any rate I saw at Alexandria some dropsical and splenetic people using the mud of Egyptian earth. And many, anointing their shins and thighs and forearms and upper arms and backs and sides and chests with the mud of this earth, were clearly benefited. In the same way this mud benefits old inflammations and the loose kinds of oedema, so that I know some who had become swollen in their whole habit as a result of immoderate evacuation from haemorrhoids who were manifestly benefited. And some completely cured chronic pains fixed in some part with this mud; for all earth has a drying power, since by nature its body is dry, and when it is exactly unmixed with fiery substance, it dries without the least biting; and its having been washed contributes to this.
