response.translation: [9.1.3] [3. On the washing of earth.] All earth is washed in the same manner as that previously described for the Lemnian: first it is kneaded up with water that has no indication of any medicinal quality; then, when the mud has settled and the water has been removed from above, next that which lies beneath it is separated from the stony and sandy matter settling at the bottom. And if you have a trained gustatory sense, you yourself will be an accurate judge of which earth needs to be washed and which does not. For some do not need washing, while some need to be washed twice or three times. The Lemnian, then, you receive ready, washed once by the priestess, and not needing to be washed a second time.

raw_text: {"translation": "[9.1.4] [4. On Samian earth.] Samian earth does not even need to be washed. We use rather the one of its two kinds which they also call the Samian star, for spittings of blood, from whatever source they happen to arise, just as we use the Lemnian seal. By the same power they also help haemorrhages from the womb and the so-called female flux, and indeed also dysenteric ulcerations before the ulcers become putrefactive; it is the custom of physicians to call such conditions nomai, from the putrefaction 'grazing' (nemesthai) upon the neighbouring parts, destroying them along with the part first damaged. I have sometimes used the Lemnian earth too in such cases, and it clearly did good both when injected through the seat and when drunk, the ulcers having first been washed out, as we are accustomed to do, first with a fairly undiluted melikraton, and second with brine. It was injected, then, in juice of plantain, and it was drunk in watery oxykraton (vinegar-and-water). The Lemnian earth appears to have a power not a little more active than the Samian, which is why parts that have already become inflamed do not tolerate its power, but are plainly made rough, and most of all when the person is soft-fleshed. Whereas by the Samian earth not only is none of the parts in such a state exacerbated, but it is actually soothed, and most of all the hotter and more flaccid parts, such as the breasts and the testicles and the glands. In such a case you would use this sort of earth suitably if, after grinding it fine in water, you mix in as much good rose oil as will, once mixed in, not allow the drug to dry out. What is prepared in this way is good also for the other inflammations that are hot, and for incipient buboes and gouty fluxes, and in general wherever we wish to cool moderately while soothing, so that the power of the Samian earth is manifestly shown to be moderately cooling. Its substance is also somewhat more airy when compared with the Lemnian, as its lightness shows. By these marks, then, test every other medicinal earth as well. By marks I mean the lightness and heaviness in its consistency, and the roughness and smoothness in its taste, and in addition the glutinous and the cleansing quality. For the Samian star is glue-holding and viscous, the Lemnian seal also having a little of this sort of quality. Both Selinusian and Chian earth have a cleansing power, and a moderate one, which is why some women use them on the face. It has been shown in the third book of the Method of Healing that everything that is slightly cleansing is suited to the fleshing-over of ulcers, and if it dries, it is also good for cicatrization; and the most suitable of these for superficial ulcers and burns are those which, in addition to drying without biting, neither heat nor cool perceptibly. Hence Selinusian and Chian earth are the finest drugs for burn ulcers; for these require drugs that cleanse most moderately without conspicuous warming or cooling, which is the case with Selinusian and Chian and Samian earth. It has been said that the so-called star is also a kind of the latter, surpassing the other earth in having something viscous and glutinous, which is why neither for other ulcers nor for burns is it a match for the others, those at least which do not have the glutinous quality. For the glutinous quality makes the substance more clogging, so that it does not cleanse, at least whenever no other pungency is present in addition to the viscous and glutinous body, as there is in bird-lime. Chian and Selinusian earth, however, fall short of the Samian for incipient inflammations about the breasts and testicles and groins. Nevertheless they are not unsuitable, when nothing else of those that act perfectly is at hand. Cimolian earth, being of mixed power, has something cooling, but also something slightly dispersing; hence when washed it lays this aside, while without being washed it acts by both powers, just as many other compound drugs do which both disperse and repel. And according to the nature of the liquids mixed with it, it manifestly displays each of its two powers. For mixed with repellent and cooling liquids it renders the mud produced from itself and them cooling and repellent, and with dispersing ones it renders it dispersing as well. In this way, at any rate, it also suits burns, and some laymen smear it on, having kneaded it on the spot with vinegar. In such use the vinegar should not be too pungent; and if it should be so, it is better to mix water with it. Remember, however, that this is common to every light earth: for all of them benefit burns when smeared on at once with vinegar or oxykraton, preventing them from blistering. In this one must look also to the nature of the body being treated, whether it is soft or hard, always knowing this as a general principle, that soft bodies do not tolerate the power of strong drugs, whereas hard bodies tolerate it. These matters, however, are not proper to the present treatise; for they will be spoken of at greater length both in the books on the composition of drugs and in those on readily available remedies. The present exposition has from the beginning striven to discover the general powers of drugs, attending to which a person will have very ample resources for their particular use, provided of course he has learnt in addition the method of using them; so that it is no longer fitting to prolong matters, but, as was said before, to recall now too that earth itself, unmixed with any other substance of a different kind, is of a drying power without biting. But since it is impossible to find any body that is exactly unmixed, it is fitting to examine in addition the admixture of what has come to be attached to it, according to the differences in lightness and heaviness and those in taste. For if it has some suggestion of astringency, it has taken on as much coldness as astringency; and if some pungency should appear, it has as much heat as pungency. One must consider in the same way in the case of light and heavy earth: the light earth becoming such whenever it partakes of abundant airy substance in the mixture throughout its whole self, while the heavy, the more it is such, by so much the more is a purer earth. It is a property of earth not to melt when it comes near fire, which lead and tin, silver and gold do have; so that when you hear of a silver-earth or gold-earth or iron-earth—for some so name those taken from the mines—do not suppose that the silver or the gold or the iron is blended through and through with the earth, but that small particles lie near small particles of the earth, mixed in with them, of gold in the gold-earth, of silver in the silver-earth, of iron in the iron-earth, and that these, being melted by the fire in the furnaces, come together with one another. In the same way the earth that contains glass is sandy, for it is in sand especially that small grains of this kind of substance are often found. And those experienced in these matters, on seeing such sands, recognize how much glass they can gather from them; and many small grains of gold are found in certain sands, but those who occupy themselves with these things do not extract the gold and the glass from every sand, choosing, of course, those which yield the most at little expense, since to spend a great deal in the furnaces and obtain a trifle of the substance collected seems to them unprofitable. For this reason, then, although many sands contain grains of gold and glass, those skilled in these matters do not go to all of them. By the same reasoning they do not pick out copper or silver or iron or tin or lead from every earth. Nor indeed, when they separate each of the things mentioned from the earth mixed with it, is the residue like the other earths, which I said are customarily so named by all Greeks, having as a common mark that they are soaked through and easily dissolve into mud. For the residue of the earth in the mines becomes stony, unmeltable and not to be soaked through. By 'being soaked through' I mean being moistened through the whole substance, and by 'being wetted' being moistened on the outer surface alone, the moisture not penetrating to its depth. Thus too the mined cadmia is produced, being stony and not to be soaked through. But about such bodies we shall speak in due course; now I shall return again to medicinal earth, which, because it readily dissolves into mud when soaked in water, is for this reason named earth, and because we have need of it as of other drugs, for this reason might reasonably be called pharmakitis. And yet some call only the so-called ampelitis earth pharmakitis, either as being the only one of this kind or as having the medicinal power more effectively, which is indeed true. It is named ampelitis not because it is better to plant vines in it, but because, smeared around the vines, it destroys the worms that breed on them, which the vine-dressers in our country call sknipes. These are bred when spring sets in, when the vines sprout, and especially the swelling part of them from which the shoot grows, which they call the eye. By eating through these eyes, then, the sknipes do no small harm to the vines, which is why those skilled in these matters smear the roots of these eyes. On this account, then, such earth is called both ampelitis and pharmakitis, showing from its destruction of the sknipes too how much medicinal power it possesses. It stands far apart also from the other kinds of earth which we use for cures, coming already near to the stony. Hence you will find it mixed in the prescriptions of drugs where it is fitting to dry and disperse something. For it does not have the non-biting, moderate and soothing quality like the Chian and Samian and Selinusian. Of the Cimolian also it has been said before that it is slightly stronger than these, but still non-biting itself too, and especially if it has been washed. The Cretan earth too is somewhat like these, but it is quite weak, having much of the airy, yet it has the cleansing quality, which is why people brighten dirty silverware with it; so that you might have this too for the purpose for which we have said before that the others which cleanse without biting are suitable. Of all these the Lemnian has a stronger power, for there is present in it also something of astringency, and the Eretrian a still stronger one than this, though not so as actually to bite. And if it is washed too, it becomes quite moderate, like those mentioned before. It is possible for this earth to be washed not once but even two or three times, as also the Cimolian. And indeed some also burn it, making it evidently more fine-particled and more pungent, so that it passes over into the dispersing power. And if, having been burnt, it is washed, leaving the pungency behind in the water but keeping the fine-particled quality from the roasting, it becomes more drying. Hence, whereas unburnt earth of every kind is, by the common account, useful for ulcers, that which has been washed after being burnt is even more so, and is useful also for ulcers that are hard to flesh over and hard to cicatrize. There being two kinds of it, the one ash-coloured in hue is better than the very white. There is also another earth called pnigitis, resembling the Cimolian in its whole power but differing in colour, for it is black, like the ampelitis, and it has the viscous and glutinous quality no less than Samian earth, but sometimes even more. There was also given to us, in this great plague, another earth from the part of Armenia bordering on Cappadocia, more drying, yellowish-ochre in colour; the one who gave it called it a stone, not an earth, and it is extremely smooth, like lime too—I so name, obviously, burnt rock. But just as nothing sandy is carried along in that, so neither in the Armenian; for after being broken up with the pestle in the mortar it is as smooth and stone-free as lime and the Samian star, though not equally light with the star. Hence it is also more compact than it and less airy, and for this reason gives those who look at it more carelessly the impression of being a stone. It makes no difference for present purposes whether one calls it a stone or an earth, knowing that it dries in the highest degree. For in dysenteries and fluxes of the belly, and spitting of blood and catarrh, and in addition putrefactive ulcers in the mouth, it is most suitable. And indeed it greatly benefits those who suffer fluxes from the head into the chest, so that it also strongly helps those who are continually short of breath for such a cause. And indeed those who labour under consumption—these too it benefits. For it dries their ulcer, so that they no longer even cough, unless they should err considerably in their regimen or the surrounding air should suddenly fall into a bad mixture. And it seems to me that, just as we have often observed in the case of fistulas, not only in other parts but also at the seat, that without inserting a collyrium that removes the filth or the callus from the fistula, by the drying drug alone they are brought together and closed, so it happens also in the case of the ulcer in the lung. For this too appears to be benefited in like manner by drying drugs, whenever it is moderate and not very large; so that some of those who had them thought they had been completely rid of them, and of those who travelled from Rome to Libya for such a cause some were completely persuaded that they were healthy, and for some years passed their lives without complaint, and then at some later time, when they had lived a less guarded regimen, a relapse of the disease occurred. These, then, as I said, the bole from Armenia manifestly helped, even though they were living in Rome, and still more those continually short of breath. And in this great plague, which is similar in form to the one that occurred in Thucydides' time, all who drank this drug were cured quickly, while all those whom it did not benefit died, nor were they helped by anything else; from which it is clear that it failed to help only those who were in an incurable state. It is drunk with wine thin in consistency, moderately mixed if the person is entirely free of fever or feverish only slightly, but quite watery if he is more strongly feverish. Nor indeed are the pestilential fevers violent in their heat. As for ulcers that need to be dried, what need is there even to say how great a power this Armenian bole has? For the Samian star is glue-holding and viscous, the Lemnian seal also having a little of this sort of quality. Both Selinusian and Chian earth have a cleansing power, and a moderate one, which is why some women use them on the face. It has been shown in the third book of the Method of Healing that everything that is slightly cleansing is suited to the fleshing-over of ulcers, and if it dries, it is also good for cicatrization; and the most suitable of these for superficial ulcers and burns are those which, in addition to drying without biting, neither heat nor cool perceptibly. Hence Selinusian and Chian earth are the finest drugs for burn ulcers; for these require drugs that cleanse most moderately without conspicuous warming or cooling, which is the case with Selinusian and Chian and Samian earth. It has been said that the so-called star is also a kind of the latter, surpassing the other earth in having something viscous and glutinous, which is why neither for other ulcers nor for burns is it a match for the others, those at least which do not have the glutinous quality. For the glutinous quality makes the substance more clogging, so that it does not cleanse, at least whenever no other pungency is present in addition to the viscous and glutinous body, as there is in bird-lime. Chian and Selinusian earth, however, fall short of the Samian for incipient inflammations about the breasts and testicles and groins. Nevertheless they are not unsuitable, when nothing else of those that act perfectly is at hand. Cimolian earth, being of mixed power, has something cooling, but also something slightly dispersing; hence when washed it lays this aside, while without being washed it acts by both powers, just as many other compound drugs do which both disperse and repel. And according to the nature of the liquids mixed with it, it manifestly displays each of its two powers. For mixed with repellent and cooling liquids it renders the mud produced from itself and them cooling and repellent, and with dispersing ones it renders it dispersing as well. In this way, at any rate, it also suits burns, and some laymen smear it on, having kneaded it on the spot with vinegar. In such use the vinegar should not be too pungent; and if it should be so, it is better to mix water with it. Remember, however, that this is common to every light earth: for all of them benefit burns when smeared on at once with vinegar or oxykraton, preventing them from blistering. In this one must look also to the nature of the body being treated, whether it is soft or hard, always knowing this as a general principle, that soft bodies do not tolerate the power of strong drugs, whereas hard bodies tolerate it. These matters, however, are not proper to the present treatise; for they will be spoken of at greater length both in the books on the composition of drugs and in those on readily available remedies. The present exposition has from the beginning striven to discover the general powers of drugs, attending to which a person will have very ample resources for their particular use, provided of course he has learnt in addition the method of using them; so that it is no longer fitting to prolong matters, but, as was said before, to recall now too that earth itself, unmixed with any other substance of a different kind, is of a drying power without biting. But since it is impossible to find any body that is exactly unmixed, it is fitting to examine in addition the admixture of what has come to be attached to it, according to the differences in lightness and heaviness and those in taste. For if it has some suggestion of astringency, it has taken on as much coldness as astringency; and if some pungency should appear, it has as much heat as pungency. One must consider in the same way in the case of light and heavy earth: the light earth becoming such whenever it partakes of abundant airy substance in the mixture throughout its whole self, while the heavy, the more it is such, by so much the more is a purer earth. It is a property of earth not to melt when it comes near fire, which lead and tin, silver and gold do have; so that when you hear of a silver-earth or gold-earth or iron-earth—for some so name those taken from the mines—do not suppose that the silver or the gold or the iron is blended through and through with the earth, but that small particles lie near small particles of the earth, mixed in with them, of gold in the gold-earth, of silver in the silver-earth, of iron in the iron-earth, and that these, being melted by the fire in the furnaces, come together with one another. In the same way the earth that contains glass is sandy, for it is in sand especially that small grains of this kind of substance are often found. And those experienced in these matters, on seeing such sands, recognize how much glass they can gather from them; and many small grains of gold are found in certain sands, but those who occupy themselves with these things do not extract the gold and the glass from every sand, choosing, of course, those which yield the most at little expense, since to spend a great deal in the furnaces and obtain a trifle of the substance collected seems to them unprofitable. For this reason, then, although many sands contain grains of gold and glass, those skilled in these matters do not go to all of them. By the same reasoning they do not pick out copper or silver or iron or tin or lead from every earth. Nor indeed, when they separate each of the things mentioned from the earth mixed with it, is the residue like the other earths, which I said are customarily so named by all Greeks, having as a common mark that they are soaked through and easily dissolve into mud. For the residue of the earth in the mines becomes stony, unmeltable and not to be soaked through. By 'being soaked through' I mean being moistened through the whole substance, and by 'being wetted' being moistened on the outer surface alone, the moisture not penetrating to its depth. Thus too the mined cadmia is produced, being stony and not to be soaked through. But about such bodies we shall speak in due course; now I shall return again to medicinal earth, which, because it readily dissolves into mud when soaked in water, is for this reason named earth, and because we have need of it as of other drugs, for this reason might reasonably be called pharmakitis. And yet some call only the so-called ampelitis earth pharmakitis, either as being the only one of this kind or as having the medicinal power more effectively, which is indeed true. It is named ampelitis not because it is better to plant vines in it, but because, smeared around the vines, it destroys the worms that breed on them, which the vine-dressers in our country call sknipes. These are bred when spring sets in, when the vines sprout, and especially the swelling part of them from which the shoot grows, which they call the eye. By eating through these eyes, then, the sknipes do no small harm to the vines, which is why those skilled in these matters smear the roots of these eyes. On this account, then, such earth is called both ampelitis and pharmakitis, showing from its destruction of the sknipes too how much medicinal power it possesses. It stands far apart also from the other kinds of earth which we use for cures, coming already near to the stony. Hence you will find it mixed in the prescriptions of drugs where it is fitting to dry and disperse something. For it does not have the non-biting, moderate and soothing quality like the Chian and Samian and Selinusian. Of the Cimolian also it has been said before that it is slightly stronger than these, but still non-biting itself too, and especially if it has been washed. The Cretan earth too is somewhat like these, but it is quite weak, having much of the airy, yet it has the cleansing quality, which is why people brighten dirty silverware with it; so that you might have this too for the purpose for which we have said before that the others which cleanse without biting are suitable. Of all these the Lemnian has a stronger power, for there is present in it also something of astringency, and the Eretrian a still stronger one than this, though not so as actually to bite. And if it is washed too, it becomes quite moderate, like those mentioned before. It is possible for this earth to be washed not once but even two or three times, as also the Cimolian. And indeed some also burn it, making it evidently more fine-particled and more pungent, so that it passes over into the dispersing power. And if, having been burnt, it is washed, leaving the pungency behind in the water but keeping the fine-particled quality from the roasting, it becomes more drying. Hence, whereas unburnt earth of every kind is, by the common account, useful for ulcers, that which has been washed after being burnt is even more so, and is useful also for ulcers that are hard to flesh over and hard to cicatrize. There being two kinds of it, the one ash-coloured in hue is better than the very white. There is also another earth called pnigitis, resembling the Cimolian in its whole power but differing in colour, for it is black, like the ampelitis, and it has the viscous and glutinous quality no less than Samian earth, but sometimes even more. There was also given to us, in this great plague, another earth from the part of Armenia bordering on Cappadocia, more drying, yellowish-ochre in colour; the one who gave it called it a stone, not an earth, and it is extremely smooth, like lime too—I so name, obviously, burnt rock. But just as nothing sandy is carried along in that, so neither in the Armenian; for after being broken up with the pestle in the mortar it is as smooth and stone-free as lime and the Samian star, though not equally light with the star. Hence it is also more compact than it and less airy, and for this reason gives those who look at it more carelessly the impression of being a stone. It makes no difference for present purposes whether one calls it a stone or an earth, knowing that it dries in the highest degree. For in dysenteries and fluxes of the belly, and spitting of blood and catarrh, and in addition putrefactive ulcers in the mouth, it is most suitable. And indeed it greatly benefits those who suffer fluxes from the head into the chest, so that it also strongly helps those who are continually short of breath for such a cause. And indeed those who labour under consumption—these too it benefits. For it dries their ulcer, so that they no longer even cough, unless they should err considerably in their regimen or the surrounding air should suddenly fall into a bad mixture. And it seems to me that, just as we have often observed in the case of fistulas, not only in other parts but also at the seat, that without inserting a collyrium that removes the filth or the callus from the fistula, by the drying drug alone they are brought together and closed, so it happens also in the case of the ulcer in the lung. For this too appears to be benefited in like manner by drying drugs, whenever it is moderate and not very large; so that some of those who had them thought they had been completely rid of them, and of those who travelled from Rome to Libya for such a cause some were completely persuaded that they were healthy, and for some years passed their lives without complaint, and then at some later time, when they had lived a less guarded regimen, a relapse of the disease occurred. These, then, as I said, the bole from Armenia manifestly helped, even though they were living in Rome, and still more those continually short of breath. And in this great plague, which is similar in form to the one that occurred in Thucydides' time, all who drank this drug were cured quickly, while all those whom it did not benefit died, nor were they helped by anything else; from which it is clear that it failed to help only those who were in an incurable state. It is drunk with wine thin in consistency, moderately mixed if the person is entirely free of fever or feverish only slightly, but quite watery if he is more strongly feverish. Nor indeed are the pestilential fevers violent in their heat. As for ulcers that need to be dried, what need is there even to say how great a power this Armenian bole has? You may call it, as I said, both a stone, as the one who gave it named it, and an earth, as I would say, since it is also soaked through by liquids.

response.translation: [9.2.2] [2. On haematites, galactites and melitites.] One among stones of this kind is also the one called haematites, so named from its resemblance in colour, just as also the galactites, since that one too, when dissolved into a juice, appears similar to milk. Reasonably, then, physicians have ventured to mix the haematites stone into ophthalmic medicaments. And you may use it by itself as well when the eyelids have become rough: if they have become so together with inflammation, making the dilution with egg, or better still with a decoction of fenugreek; if without inflammation, with water. Always begin from a moderately liquid form, pouring it in by means of the probe; but when you see that it tolerates its power, make it ever thicker and more so. And in the end you will make it so thick as to anoint with the tip of a probe, with the eyelid turned under or turned out. This same stone, rubbed down in the same way on a whetstone, is suited to spittings of blood and to all ulcers. Ground dry so as to become powdery, it reduces overgrowths of flesh. No one, however, uses it alone by itself. But I have used it in the cases I have mentioned, having discovered its power from its quality in respect of taste, and then wishing to test by experience whether I had inferred rightly. And the very ulcers on the eyes it alone brings to cicatrization, being rubbed down, as I said a little before, and either instilled or applied beneath the lid as a salve. For I tested this too by experience.

raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.9] [9. On sulphur.] All sulphur is of drawing power, being hot in mixture and fine-particled in substance, so that it also withstands many of the venomous creatures. I myself, at any rate, have used it often in cases of the sea-stingray and the dragon-fish, and having taught certain fishermen, I heard after a time that they praised the drug greatly. The use is made both with the drug dry, sprinkled upon the puncture, and with it mixed with saliva. For having thought of this too, I found it attested by experience; and I conceived also that it would be effective moistened with urine. On cadmia.] Cadmia is produced, for one thing, in the course of the generation of copper in the furnaces, since the whole of that earth from which the copper is generated during the smelting sends up on high a kind of soot or smut—or soot and smut, however one wishes to call it. And cadmia is also found in Cyprus without a furnace, and one would rightly name such a kind a stone. At any rate, at Soli there was still very little of the cadmia produced in the smelting-works at the time when I visited the island. raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.21] [21. On misy.] Misy. At the mine in Cyprus mentioned before, in the mountains of Soli, there was a certain large house, where along the right-hand wall—though on the left relative to us who were entering—there was an entrance into the mine itself, in which I saw certain belts, as it were, extended to a very great length, three of them one upon another: the lowest that of sory, upon it that of chalcitis, then that of misy. The man who at that time was overseer of the mine, showing me these things, said: \"Just as you have now come when we are in poverty of the cadmia that is smelted in the furnaces, so you see these three established in wondrous wealth.\" And so, taking a very great quantity of it, I brought it first to Asia and from there to Rome, and I have kept it until now, about thirty years having passed in between. And by some chance the present treatise had advanced as far as the eighth book, about twenty years ago, without this ninth being added to it, because I had not yet seen some of the stones, and moreover because of the occupations that intervened on account of other matters. The man who at that time was overseer of the mine, showing me these things, said: "Just as you have now come when we are in poverty of the cadmia that is smelted in the furnaces, so you see these three established in wondrous wealth." And so, taking a very great quantity of it, I brought it first to Asia and from there to Rome, and I have kept it until now, about thirty years having passed in between. And by some chance the present treatise had advanced as far as the eighth book, about twenty years ago, without this ninth being added to it, because I had not yet seen some of the stones, and moreover because of the occupations that intervened on account of other matters. But now, as I am adding this ninth book, in the meantime there occurred by chance a most beautiful sight, such as someone might himself have contrived on purpose. Wondering, then, at its unusual compactness, and having crushed the lump, I found on the surface, all round, the misy, like a kind of efflorescence of what was within; and upon it, between chalcitis and misy, a sort of half-completed change from chalcitis into misy—for the lump was originally of chalcitis; and what was in the depth was exact chalcitis, having as yet undergone no alteration. Having seen this, then, and having reflected that in the mine too the misy is generated upon the chalcitis in this way, as verdigris upon copper, I examined the sory still preserved in my possession, to see whether it was taking on any change into chalcitis, and a slight hint of it appeared, which perhaps itself too would be able, over a long time, to attain the change into chalcitis; so that it is no wonder that the three drugs—I mean sory, chalcitis and misy—are of a power of the same kind, differing in fineness of particles and coarseness of particles. raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.23] [23. On lead.] Lead is of a cooling power. For it has not only much moist substance congealed by cooling, but also airy substance, partaking of little of the earthy. That, then, it has a very great deal of moist substance congealed by cooling, let the melting and flowing that happen to it quickly, once it comes into contact with fire, be your evidence. That it has airy substance too, this is the sign: lead alone of the things we know increases both in bulk and in weight when stored in underground rooms that have turbid air, such that the things lying in them are quickly filled with mould; and the leads that bind the feet of statues to the stones have often been seen to have increased; and some have risen to such a bulk as to hang down from the stones like ice. These, then, are plausible indications, prior to experience, of something of its moistness and coldness; the scientific and secure ones are known through experience. At any rate, if you prepare a mortar from lead and, with a leaden pestle, putting into it whatever liquid you wish, you grind in such a way that both the pestle and the lead give off a certain juice, you will find what is generated from the two of them much colder in power than the liquid happened to be. You may put in water, and thin watery wine, and oil, and anything whatever of this kind. And if you wish to make the juice still more cooling, let the oil be omphacine, or rose-oil, or quince-oil, or myrtle-oil. Using the juice generated for the inflammations in the seat that arise together with ulcers or folds, and for those in the genitals and testicles and breasts, you will have an excellent drug. Likewise also against all the other fluxes at their onset, those which fall upon the groins or the feet or the other joints, and indeed also for malignant ulcers, so that, having used it also against the cancerous ones, you will marvel at the drug. If you wish to gather quickly a very great deal of the juice of lead, try grinding in the sun or in air that has in any way become warm. The drug will be of manifold use to you if you also grind it with the cooling juices put in, such as of houseleek, cotyledon, endive, lettuce, chondrile, psyllion (fleawort), unripe grape and purslane. response.translation: [9.3.31] [31. On lime.] Lime: the unslaked kind burns violently, so as to produce an eschar; the slaked kind also produces an eschar itself at once, but after one or two days it burns less and produces an eschar less, and after a time it does not produce eschars at all. It still heats, however, and melts away the flesh. If it is washed, it deposits its biting in the water and makes what is called lye, while it itself dries without biting. And if it is washed two or three times or more often, it becomes completely free of biting and dries nobly without biting.

raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.33] [33. On phykos.] Of what sort of power phykos is will be stated in the account concerning psimythion. [9.3.34] [34. On chalkanthos.] Chalkanthos. I have also made observation concerning chalkanthos, which by chance changes into chalkitis. For I brought this drug too from Cyprus in very great quantity. And the whole of its outer part, after nearly twenty years, became chalkitis, while the inner part was still chalkanthos. For this reason I still keep up to now the piece that is changing in this way, watching how far the change advances toward the depth in each year, just as that of chalkitis into misy, as has been said before. One may marvel, in the case of this drug, how a not ignoble heat is mixed with the strongest astringency. It is clear, then, that it is able most of all things to cure moist flesh as by salting, consuming the moisture by its heat, and by its astringency drawing together and compacting the substance. For in this very action it also squeezes out something of the moisture itself, and it binds and dries and draws together toward itself the substance of the whole flesh. In Cyprus, then, at the time when I was there, I saw this drug being collected in the following manner. There was a house, large but not high, lying before the entrance to the mine. And along the left wall of this house, which was on the right hand for those entering, a tunnel had been hollowed out into the adjoining hill, in breadth such that three men could touch one another, in height such that the tallest man could walk upright. This tunnel sloped downward, but was not steep or precipitous. At its end, it being about a stade long, there was a pit full of water, greenish and thick and lukewarm. Throughout the whole descent there was a warmth similar to that in the first rooms of the baths, which they are accustomed to call promalakteria. The water collected each day was a quantity of about eight Roman amphorae, falling in small drops, in the twenty-four hours of the whole day and night, out of the hill which had been bored through. Certain fettered men, then, carrying up this water, threw it into square basins in the house lying in front, made of pottery, in which, congealing in a few days, it became chalkanthos. To me, when I went down to the end of the excavation, where the lukewarm and greenish water was collected, the smell of the air appeared stifling and hard to bear, smelling of chalkitis and ios. And the water itself, when tasted, had the same quality. For these reasons the fettered men carried up the amphorae both naked and with haste, and did not endure to remain for a longer time, but quickly ran back up, lamps burning on either side in the walls of the excavation at a measured interval, which did not themselves last for a long time either, but were extinguished very quickly. This excavation, then, I heard from them had been dug little by little over many years. For this, they said, which you now see carried down from the hill into the pit, the greenish water, is accustomed to become less than itself little by little, and when it is near to ceasing, the fettered men again dig under the adjoining part of the hill. response.translation: [9.3.38] [38. On chrysocolla.] Chrysocolla. This drug too belongs to those that melt flesh, yet it does not bite strongly; it is, however, sufficiently dispersing and drying. Some people, then, give this name only to the mined kind, while others give it to the kind prepared in a copper mortar with a copper pestle by means of a boy's urine, which some people count among the different kinds of ios (verdigris). It is better to prepare it in summer, or at any rate in warm air, grinding the urine in the mortar. It is better, too, that the copper from which you make both the mortar itself and the pestle be red; for more is rubbed off as the pestle is turned round when the copper is softer. This drug is most suitable for malignant ulcers, both by itself and mixed with others, as will be stated in the books on the composition of drugs. For now it suffices to know this much: by as much as it dries more and bites less than the mined chrysocolla, by so much does it surpass it in fineness of particles. And indeed, if you burn that mined chrysocolla itself, you will make it much more fine-particled.

response.translation: [9.3.39] [39. On psimythion.] Psimythion (white lead). This drug too bears witness to the power described before it. At any rate, although it is itself dissolved by pungent vinegar, when tasted it is nevertheless neither pungent nor biting nor dispersing, but clogging and cooling, being of a power most opposed to that of verdigris; and yet that too comes into being when vinegar dissolves the copper. When psimythion is burnt and has changed into what is called sandyx, it becomes a drug more fine-particled than itself, though not yet, however, a heating one. The phykos, for its part, while preserving the coldness of psimythion, has acquired fineness of particles, so that by means of it its power is able to sink down into the depth of the bodies it comes into contact with.

raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.40] [40. On psoricon.] Psoricon. The drug is produced when a double quantity of chalcitis is mixed with litharge, both being first ground fine in the most pungent vinegar, then put into a new pot, which you will bury for forty days in midsummer in a dung-heap. This drug becomes at once more drying and less biting than chalcitis, and evidently also more fine-particled. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 10. None of what is now to be said will bring great benefit to those ignorant of what was said at the beginning of the treatise in the first five books, and some of it will perhaps even harm the man who uses the drugs written in it without possessing a method. I shall therefore address you as one who has learned those things, having first recalled the chief point of the whole treatise. It was shown that drugs act, in respect of the qualities called active, by heat and cold and dryness and moistness, and that by the mixture of these they become acerbic and harsh and saline and salty and bitter and pungent and sweet, and some cleansing, some repelling, some drawing, some softening, some caustic, some putrefying, some escharotic, and further, in addition to these, in respect of other more specific activities, flesh-forming and cicatrizing and agglutinating of fistulas or ulcers, or reducing of overgrowing flesh. It was also shown that the universal power may be discovered by indication from a single trial—and not any chance trial, but one made together with the distinctions stated; and that once the universal power has been discovered there is no longer any need of trial as regards the particular activities, except solely for the confirmation of what reason has discovered. In this way, then, let us now too make our judgment of the material before us, and this is the material derived from animals. For in the three books following in order after the fifth, the sixth, seventh and eighth, we went through the material concerning plants—not, evidently, all that exists throughout the whole inhabited world, but as much as we ourselves have experience of. In the book before this one, the ninth of the whole treatise, the material concerning earthy and stony bodies. It remains for us still to go through the material concerning animals; then there is still left over that of the things generated in the sea and in lakes, or in general in water, which are neither plants nor earth nor stone nor animal. Such things are altogether very few and will be written last, after we have gone through what pertains to the bodies of animals. The order of teaching for these too will follow the order of the first letters in their names. And just as in the material of plants I also gave an account of the juices produced from them, so too now the teaching of the power will be not only of the solid parts in animals but also of what is contained in them: phlegm, bile, blood, urine, dung and the like. Now in what was said before, not many of the particular items in the materia written by physicians were unknown to me, but I myself took pains to know their powers through experience; and if there was any whose power I did not know, I did not write about it at all, not thinking it right to trust others even about a single thing of this kind, because I had found that some of them lie about many things. But with the material now before us it is not so. I confess that there are very many parts and fluids contained in the bodies of animals of which I myself have had no such experience as some have written of; for some of them are lewd and disgusting, and some are even forbidden by the laws—about which I do not know how Xenocrates came to write, a man who lived not long ago but in the time of our grandfathers, when the Roman empire had forbidden the eating of human beings; yet he, as though having made trial himself, writes with full confidence what affections human brain, when eaten, or flesh or liver is naturally fitted to cure, and what the bones of the head or shin or fingers cure, some burnt, some unburnt, when drunk, and what blood itself cures. These things, then, even if contrary to the laws, are at least not lewd. But the drinking of sweat and urine and a woman's menstrual blood is lewd and disgusting, and no less than these dung, of which Xenocrates wrote what it is able to do when smeared on the parts about the mouth and the throat and swallowed down into the belly; he has written also about the filth in the ears being swallowed. I for my part would not have endured to swallow even this, on condition of never falling ill; and I consider dung far more disgusting than it. And it is a greater reproach for a man of sound mind to be called a dung-eater than a performer of shameful acts or a catamite; indeed even among performers of shameful acts we loathe those who phoenicize more than those who lesbianize, and the man who drinks menstrual blood seems to me to suffer something similar to the former. Neither, then, would any human being in his natural condition endure to come to the trial of these, nor of those things which are more moderate than these yet still lewd—to smear some part of the body with dung on account of the affection in it, or with human semen. Xenocrates is accustomed to call it gonos, and he distinguishes with all care what the gonos by itself alone is naturally fitted to help when smeared on, and what it helps after the intercourse of man and woman, when it has fallen out of the woman's vagina. For there must have arisen some great poverty of remedies, for someone to treat chilblains with a man's semen that did not remain inside but flowed out of the woman upon intercourse. Indeed much of this kind of material is in what he has written about the benefit derived from animals. For it is not only of man, evidently, that he recounts what power urine has when drunk, or dung when swallowed and smeared on the parts in the mouth, but of each of the other animals as well, and much else besides of things hard to procure, as when he mentions the elephant or the Nile horse. As for the basilisk, I have never even seen the beast, and if what is said about it is true, it is dangerous even to come near this animal. Others too wrote things similar to Xenocrates about animals, from whom Xenocrates himself also copied out the most part. For whence could he have had the means himself to make trial of so many things and of such a kind? At any rate our own Attalus, who was once king, appears to write less, although he was most ambitious concerning the trial of such things. And someone, praising the same kind of treatise by Ateuristus, gave me that too to read through—a work produced, as it seems to me at least, without the personal observation of its author. I therefore shall mention neither basilisks nor elephants nor Nile horses nor anything else of which I have no experience myself; and as for the so-called philtres, attracting-charms, dream-senders and hate-charms—for I deliberately use their own names for them—I would not have mentioned them in writing at all, even if I had sufficient experience, just as I would not deadly drugs or those which, as they themselves call them, are affection-producing. For some of those are even ridiculous: to bind one's opponents at law so that they can utter nothing in the court, or to make the pregnant woman miscarry, or never conceive, and all other such things. Most of these are indeed also impossible by the test of experience, and some, even if possible, are at any rate harmful to the life of men; so that I, by the gods, wonder with what thought some men came to write them. For things which bring disrepute to the living when known—how did they hope that these would bring them good repute after death? If, being kings among men, they made trial of them on those condemned to death, they did nothing terrible. But since private persons, having had no such authority in their whole life, came to write them, one of two things follows: either, not having made trial themselves, they write about what they do not know, or, if they did make trial, they are the most impious of all men, having given destructive drugs for the sake of trial to those who had done no wrong, and sometimes even to fine and good men. response.translation: [9.3.40] [40. On psoricon.] Psoricon. The drug is produced when a double quantity of chalcitis is mixed with litharge, both being first ground fine in the most pungent vinegar, then put into a new pot, which you will bury for forty days in midsummer in a dung-heap. This drug becomes at once more drying and less biting than chalcitis, and evidently also more fine-particled. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 10. None of what is now to be said will bring great benefit to those ignorant of what was said at the beginning of the treatise in the first five books, and some of it will perhaps even harm the man who uses the drugs written in it without possessing a method. I shall therefore address you as one who has learned those things, having first recalled the chief point of the whole treatise. It was shown that drugs act, in respect of the qualities called active, by heat and cold and dryness and moistness, and that by the mixture of these they become acerbic and harsh and saline and salty and bitter and pungent and sweet, and some cleansing, some repelling, some drawing, some softening, some caustic, some putrefying, some escharotic, and further, in addition to these, in respect of other more specific activities, flesh-forming and cicatrizing and agglutinating of fistulas or ulcers, or reducing of overgrowing flesh. It was also shown that the universal power may be discovered by indication from a single trial—and not any chance trial, but one made together with the distinctions stated; and that once the universal power has been discovered there is no longer any need of trial as regards the particular activities, except solely for the confirmation of what reason has discovered. In this way, then, let us now too make our judgment of the material before us, and this is the material derived from animals. For in the three books following in order after the fifth, the sixth, seventh and eighth, we went through the material concerning plants—not, evidently, all that exists throughout the whole inhabited world, but as much as we ourselves have experience of. In the book before this one, the ninth of the whole treatise, the material concerning earthy and stony bodies. It remains for us still to go through the material concerning animals; then there is still left over that of the things generated in the sea and in lakes, or in general in water, which are neither plants nor earth nor stone nor animal. Such things are altogether very few and will be written last, after we have gone through what pertains to the bodies of animals. The order of teaching for these too will follow the order of the first letters in their names. And just as in the material of plants I also gave an account of the juices produced from them, so too now the teaching of the power will be not only of the solid parts in animals but also of what is contained in them: phlegm, bile, blood, urine, dung and the like. Now in what was said before, not many of the particular items in the materia written by physicians were unknown to me, but I myself took pains to know their powers through experience; and if there was any whose power I did not know, I did not write about it at all, not thinking it right to trust others even about a single thing of this kind, because I had found that some of them lie about many things. But with the material now before us it is not so. I confess that there are very many parts and fluids contained in the bodies of animals of which I myself have had no such experience as some have written of; for some of them are lewd and disgusting, and some are even forbidden by the laws—about which I do not know how Xenocrates came to write, a man who lived not long ago but in the time of our grandfathers, when the Roman empire had forbidden the eating of human beings; yet he, as though having made trial himself, writes with full confidence what affections human brain, when eaten, or flesh or liver is naturally fitted to cure, and what the bones of the head or shin or fingers cure, some burnt, some unburnt, when drunk, and what blood itself cures. These things, then, even if contrary to the laws, are at least not lewd. But the drinking of sweat and urine and a woman's menstrual blood is lewd and disgusting, and no less than these dung, of which Xenocrates wrote what it is able to do when smeared on the parts about the mouth and the throat and swallowed down into the belly; he has written also about the filth in the ears being swallowed. I for my part would not have endured to swallow even this, on condition of never falling ill; and I consider dung far more disgusting than it. And it is a greater reproach for a man of sound mind to be called a dung-eater than a performer of shameful acts or a catamite; indeed even among performers of shameful acts we loathe those who phoenicize more than those who lesbianize, and the man who drinks menstrual blood seems to me to suffer something similar to the former. Neither, then, would any human being in his natural condition endure to come to the trial of these, nor of those things which are more moderate than these yet still lewd—to smear some part of the body with dung on account of the affection in it, or with human semen. Xenocrates is accustomed to call it gonos, and he distinguishes with all care what the gonos by itself alone is naturally fitted to help when smeared on, and what it helps after the intercourse of man and woman, when it has fallen out of the woman's vagina. For there must have arisen some great poverty of remedies, for someone to treat chilblains with a man's semen that did not remain inside but flowed out of the woman upon intercourse. Indeed much of this kind of material is in what he has written about the benefit derived from animals. For it is not only of man, evidently, that he recounts what power urine has when drunk, or dung when swallowed and smeared on the parts in the mouth, but of each of the other animals as well, and much else besides of things hard to procure, as when he mentions the elephant or the Nile horse. As for the basilisk, I have never even seen the beast, and if what is said about it is true, it is dangerous even to come near this animal. Others too wrote things similar to Xenocrates about animals, from whom Xenocrates himself also copied out the most part. For whence could he have had the means himself to make trial of so many things and of such a kind? At any rate our own Attalus, who was once king, appears to write less, although he was most ambitious concerning the trial of such things. And someone, praising the same kind of treatise by Ateuristus, gave me that too to read through—a work produced, as it seems to me at least, without the personal observation of its author. I therefore shall mention neither basilisks nor elephants nor Nile horses nor anything else of which I have no experience myself; and as for the so-called philtres, attracting-charms, dream-senders and hate-charms—for I deliberately use their own names for them—I would not have mentioned them in writing at all, even if I had sufficient experience, just as I would not deadly drugs or those which, as they themselves call them, are affection-producing. For some of those are even ridiculous: to bind one's opponents at law so that they can utter nothing in the court, or to make the pregnant woman miscarry, or never conceive, and all other such things. Most of these are indeed also impossible by the test of experience, and some, even if possible, are at any rate harmful to the life of men; so that I, by the gods, wonder with what thought some men came to write them. For things which bring disrepute to the living when known—how did they hope that these would bring them good repute after death? If, being kings among men, they made trial of them on those condemned to death, they did nothing terrible. But since private persons, having had no such authority in their whole life, came to write them, one of two things follows: either, not having made trial themselves, they write about what they do not know, or, if they did make trial, they are the most impious of all men, having given destructive drugs for the sake of trial to those who had done no wrong, and sometimes even to fine and good men. For instance, someone, seeing two physicians standing by the dealers in petty wares, brought them honey, pretending to sell it. They tasted it and were discussing the price, and as they offered little, he hastened off and withdrew, and neither of the physicians survived. For all such things, then, it is right to hate those who wrote them no less than those who did them, but even more, in proportion as it is a lesser wrong to do some evil alone than together with many. And with the doer his acquaintance with evil theorems died too, but that of all who wrote is immortal, furnishing weapons of wrongdoing to the wicked. raw_text: {"translation": "[8.16.25] [25. On the plane tree.] The plane tree is of a moister and colder substance, not by any great margin, than the moderate ones. For this reason its green leaves, when pounded fine and applied as a plaster, give manifest benefit to inflammations in their beginning. And for this reason, when washed, it becomes a drying drug without biting, and the more so if it is washed twice or even three times. It becomes sufficiently dispersing when washed with sea-water. raw_text: {"translation": "[8.19.8] [8. On tragacanth.] Tragacanth has a power similar to that of gum, a certain clogging quality and a rather blunted pungency. And indeed it also dries in much the same way as that does. [8.19.9] [9. On tragion.] Of tragion, the leaves, the fruit and the tear (gum) are of a drawing and dispersing power. raw_text: {"translation": "[8.21.6] [6. On the date palm.] The date palm, the tree, partakes of astringent power in all its parts. Thus the juice of the branches is harsh, being composed of a watery substance that is lukewarm and an earthy substance that is cold. Of a similar nature to this is also what is called the \"brain,\" which is edible. Its fruit, and especially the sweet kind, has partaken of no small heat. Being edible, it comes into much use, not only when applied externally, where we need to tone something and to dry and to draw together and to compact and to condense, but also when taken as food, both together with other things and by itself. What they call elate, the tender shoot of the date palm, has the same power as the brain within it. Whence that one, inasmuch as it is coarse-particled, is biting and mouth-opening, and for this reason at once irritating to ulcers and productive of inflammation. The oil-like kedrea, on the other hand, is mild in power to such an extent that laymen, having learned by experience, treat the wounds inflicted on sheep being shorn by the shears by smearing it on, as they do also liquid pitch. raw_text: {"translation": "[7.10.43] [43. On coriander.] Coriander (korianon), or korion, or however you wish to name it — for the ancient Greeks call it korianon, whereas all the more recent physicians name it korion, as does Dioscorides, who says, not correctly, that the herb is cooling. For it is composed of opposite powers, having much bitter substance, which was shown to be fine-particled and earthy, and also not a little watery moisture that is lukewarm in power; and it also has something of a slight astringency. From all of these it acts in the various ways that Dioscorides wrote of, but certainly not by cooling alone. But I shall set out the cause of each of its particular actions, even though I had proposed in the present treatise to go through my own opinion only. Yet perhaps nothing will prevent it — rather, if the truth must be told, what is said in this manner about a few drugs will both be of some benefit and will recall to mind the methods set out earlier. First, then, not only Dioscorides but many other physicians too make pronouncements about diseases without drawing distinctions, just as indeed among those of the present day one can find not a few physicians of good repute who, beyond all else, go most gravely astray in this respect. For sometimes, when the part that has had the erysipelas has become black and livid and cold and no longer needs the cooling drugs as before, but now those that evacuate the humour lodged contrary to nature in the region, these men still cool it; and sometimes they pass over to the dispersing drugs, and yet say they are curing erysipelas. And indeed they write some drugs for cases of erysipelas that are still beginning and increasing, and others for those in decline. But this is not how it is. raw_text: {"translation": "[7.10.55] [55. On lily.] Of the lily, the flower is mixed in its temperament, from a certain fine-particled and earthy substance, from which it also has its bitterness in taste, and from a certain well-tempered watery substance. Hence both the oil made from it and the perfume are of a non-biting dispersing and softening power, as a result of which it is also most suitable for hardnesses in the womb; and the root and the leaves, ground fine by themselves, dry and cleanse and disperse moderately. So at any rate it is also fitting for burns; for these too require a power that is moderately drying and at the same time cleansing. Accordingly, having roasted the root and then ground it fine together with rose-oil, they apply it to burns until cicatrization. For it is also in other respects a good drug for bringing all ulcers to cicatrization. Moreover, it also softens the womb and draws forth the menses. The leaves they boil beforehand and apply, these too, until cicatrization, not only to burns but also to the other ulcers. And some also preserve them in vinegar and use them as wound-remedies. More will be said by us too about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs and in that on readily available remedies, and sometimes also in the books of the Therapeutic Method, whenever the need calls. Of the same power too is its rubbing (τρίψις), having taken it on, just as the flesh-forming and the biting. That such a rank is assessed in relation to the well-tempered nature has been said often before. And we discovered its mixture not least by judging from taste too, for it is sufficiently bitter. And such a flavour was shown to be earthy in substance, but to be thinned by abundant heat, so that it both heats and dries not ignobly. Nevertheless, also by the distinguished experience, about which much has been said before, having tested it accurately, we found this drug to be of the same mixture. For whether, having pounded the foliage together with the flowers—for the rest of it, the stalk, is useless—you sprinkle it on a clean ulcer, it appears biting and irritating; or whether, having steeped it in oil, you wish to foment either the head or the belly, it will be found to heat vigorously. And indeed those who are seized periodically by rigors, if you rub these too before the onset, they shiver less, and it does not escape the perception, immediately upon being applied, that it heats. That it is likely to kill worms, being bitter, is quite clear even before experience, if we remember what was said in the fourth of these commentaries about the nature of the bitter flavour. And you will know at once that it also has a certain dispersing and cutting power. But also that this must necessarily belong to it more than to apsinthion you will be able to reason out, first from the taste. For abrotonon partakes of some very slight acerbity, but apsinthion of not a little; and then also from the fact that abrotonon is bad for the stomach, as indeed seriphon is too, while apsinthion is good for the stomach. For it was shown about these too before that the bitter in and of itself would be entirely bad for the stomach, but the harsh or the acerbic or in general the astringent good for the stomach. And when the qualities are mixed with one another, the more vigorous would prevail. These things, then, suffice for you to know in this treatise. For it will be shown in the books of the Therapeutic Method how one might best use such a drug. And for this reason no longer seek to hear either that, applied as a plaster with boiled quince or with bread, it cures inflammations of the eyes, or that it disperses tumours (φύματα) when boiled smooth with raw barley meal. For neither of these two nor any of the others is proper to the present treatise, but for those who produce an empirical teaching it is written among the readily available drugs, whereas those who wish to practise the art rationally have need of the Therapeutic Method. For, among other things, one might be harmed rather than helped by such a history. To Hippocrates, then, writing in the Aphorisms, 'pains of the eyes drinking of unmixed wine, or a bath, or fomentation, or phlebotomy, or purging resolves', and yet not adding which pains, then, drinking of unmixed wine resolves, which a bath, and which fomentation, which phlebotomy, which purging, one would, I think, grant pardon for three reasons. For he was producing an aphoristic teaching, in which, on account of its conciseness, he has allowed many things to be said thus, and he wrote all the remedies of pains, even if he did not distinguish for which sort of pain which of them is fitting; and also in many places in his other writings he gave us starting-points for the distinctions in what was said in this way. But those who have written neither in other books about such aphorisms nor in a detailed and long treatise, write aphoristically and briefly, and if in addition to these they indicate one thing out of many, they harm us in more respects than they help. For since there are many differences among ophthalmias, and one of them needs the aforementioned plaster while the others are harmed, he who uses it in all cases without distinction will harm many more than he helps. In this manner, then, we must write not only about abrotonon but also about all the others, discovering the powers in respect of heating and cooling or moistening or drying from the methods I have often stated, but whatever is accomplished according to the peculiarity of the whole substance by experience alone. It has been shown about such things too that they are deleterious, and antidotes to deleterious things, and cathartic. For of these it is not possible to make the discovery rational, but only to find a certain plausible suspicion in some cases—not indeed in all, as this very thing too has been shown through the foregoing. But about the powers discovered in this way I shall make my discussion separately in what follows, once I have first gone through, for each species of drug, those concerning heating and cooling, moistening and drying, and whatever follows upon these. Having added, however, just so much more about abrotonon, I shall bring the discussion to an end: that the most admirable Pamphilus, although writing this herb first and perhaps, if of none of those following, at least of this one having wished to become an eyewitness, has nonetheless erred very greatly in thinking that the plant is called santonicum by the Romans. For abrotonon differs from santonicum, as Dioscorides too wrote most accurately in the third book On Materials, and all physicians and dealers in sundries know this at least. For of abrotonon there are two species, the one considered male, the other female, as this too has been distinguished in Dioscorides and Pamphilus and countless others. Different from it is apsinthion, of which again one must posit species, themselves three, of which the one is called homonymously with the genus apsinthion, of which kind the Pontic especially is, another seriphon, another santonicum. But if one should say that apsinthion is one thing, seriphon another, and santonicum another, it makes no difference for the present purposes. For we have not come to divide a name, but we are concerned about the things themselves. Since, then, these too are clearly different from one another in their forms and their tastes and their powers, let anyone, if he wishes, name them all by a single appellation, but let him teach the powers accurately. We, then, said that the forms have been sufficiently stated by Dioscorides and not a few others, so that one need not write again what has been correctly said by one's predecessors. But if those men left anything undistinguished in the powers of this plant, for the sake of which indeed I have come to this digression, I shall try to add it. Apsinthion is less hot than those mentioned, as partaking of the most astringency. And if this too is less fine-particled than they, it is also thinning, in the same manner, less than they, yet not indeed less drying. Of the others, santonicum, having its name from the Santonian country in which it grows, is nearest in power to seriphon, falling short by some little in thinning and heating and drying. And for this reason no longer seek to hear either that, applied as a plaster with boiled quince or with bread, it cures inflammations of the eyes, or that it disperses tumours (φύματα) when boiled smooth with raw barley meal. For neither of these two nor any of the others is proper to the present treatise, but for those who produce an empirical teaching it is written among the readily available drugs, whereas those who wish to practise the art rationally have need of the Therapeutic Method. For, among other things, one might be harmed rather than helped by such a history. To Hippocrates, then, writing in the Aphorisms, 'pains of the eyes drinking of unmixed wine, or a bath, or fomentation, or phlebotomy, or purging resolves', and yet not adding which pains, then, drinking of unmixed wine resolves, which a bath, and which fomentation, which phlebotomy, which purging, one would, I think, grant pardon for three reasons. For he was producing an aphoristic teaching, in which, on account of its conciseness, he has allowed many things to be said thus, and he wrote all the remedies of pains, even if he did not distinguish for which sort of pain which of them is fitting; and also in many places in his other writings he gave us starting-points for the distinctions in what was said in this way. But those who have written neither in other books about such aphorisms nor in a detailed and long treatise, write aphoristically and briefly, and if in addition to these they indicate one thing out of many, they harm us in more respects than they help. For since there are many differences among ophthalmias, and one of them needs the aforementioned plaster while the others are harmed, he who uses it in all cases without distinction will harm many more than he helps. In this manner, then, we must write not only about abrotonon but also about all the others, discovering the powers in respect of heating and cooling or moistening or drying from the methods I have often stated, but whatever is accomplished according to the peculiarity of the whole substance by experience alone. It has been shown about such things too that they are deleterious, and antidotes to deleterious things, and cathartic. For of these it is not possible to make the discovery rational, but only to find a certain plausible suspicion in some cases—not indeed in all, as this very thing too has been shown through the foregoing. But about the powers discovered in this way I shall make my discussion separately in what follows, once I have first gone through, for each species of drug, those concerning heating and cooling, moistening and drying, and whatever follows upon these. Having added, however, just so much more about abrotonon, I shall bring the discussion to an end: that the most admirable Pamphilus, although writing this herb first and perhaps, if of none of those following, at least of this one having wished to become an eyewitness, has nonetheless erred very greatly in thinking that the plant is called santonicum by the Romans. For abrotonon differs from santonicum, as Dioscorides too wrote most accurately in the third book On Materials, and all physicians and dealers in sundries know this at least. For of abrotonon there are two species, the one considered male, the other female, as this too has been distinguished in Dioscorides and Pamphilus and countless others. Different from it is apsinthion, of which again one must posit species, themselves three, of which the one is called homonymously with the genus apsinthion, of which kind the Pontic especially is, another seriphon, another santonicum. But if one should say that apsinthion is one thing, seriphon another, and santonicum another, it makes no difference for the present purposes. For we have not come to divide a name, but we are concerned about the things themselves. Since, then, these too are clearly different from one another in their forms and their tastes and their powers, let anyone, if he wishes, name them all by a single appellation, but let him teach the powers accurately. We, then, said that the forms have been sufficiently stated by Dioscorides and not a few others, so that one need not write again what has been correctly said by one's predecessors. But if those men left anything undistinguished in the powers of this plant, for the sake of which indeed I have come to this digression, I shall try to add it. Apsinthion is less hot than those mentioned, as partaking of the most astringency. And if this too is less fine-particled than they, it is also thinning, in the same manner, less than they, yet not indeed less drying. Of the others, santonicum, having its name from the Santonian country in which it grows, is nearest in power to seriphon, falling short by some little in thinning and heating and drying. Seriphon itself is less hot than abrotonon, but hotter than apsinthion, sufficiently bad for the stomach and as displaying a certain saltiness together with bitterness, and further partaking of a little acerbity. So too abrotonon and santonicum are sufficiently bad for the stomach. For alone among them apsinthion, and especially the Pontic, is good for the stomach, because it partakes of the most astringency. Burnt abrotonon is hot and dry in power, still more than burnt dry gourd and root of dill. For those are fitting for ulcers that are moist and at the same time callused without inflammation, and for this reason especially they seem to agree with those on the foreskins of the genitals. But the ash of abrotonon is biting to all ulcers. And for this reason it is fitting also against alopecia with fine-particled oil, namely castor-oil or radish-oil or Sicyonian or old oil, and especially Sabine. And it brings forth beards that come up slowly with whichever of the oils mentioned, and no less than those when moistened with mastic-oil. For it is rarefying, in addition to being fine-particled and biting and hot, which powers of it indeed one must especially know, and no longer need anything of the particulars in this treatise.
