raw_text: {"translation": "[6.5.4] [4. On olive oil.] Oil: that from the olive, which we also call oil in the most proper sense, has had the nature of its mixture determined in the preceding books; for it was shown to be moistening and moderately hot. Such is the sweetest oil, produced especially from tree-ripened fruit. But the oil called raw-pressed and omphacine (from unripe olives), to the degree that it partakes of astringency, to that same degree partakes also of coldness. As for old oil, that which comes from sweet oil grown old is hotter and more dispersing, whereas that from raw-pressed oil, so long as it preserves something of its astringency, is of mixed power, but when it has completely cast this off, it becomes like the other. And indeed those who in the preparation throw in olive-shoots also produce an oil resembling the omphacine. One ought not to inquire how it has been prepared, but rather taste it oneself: if it shows any astringency, one should suppose that to the degree it partakes of this, to that same degree it partakes also of coldness, as does the oil brought from Iberia, which they call Spanish; but if on tasting it shows no astringency at all, but is perfectly sweet, one should consider this to be moderately hot. And if it also appears fine-particled—such is the oil that is pure and translucent to the eye, and when a small quantity, once taken up, spreads over the greatest extent of the body and remains continuous with itself, and is drunk up by the skin—one should consider this the finest and the oil that most fully possesses the excellence of oil, of the kind that the Sabine oil is. That washed oil is the least biting has been stated earlier too; and how one may best wash it I shall say in the following treatise, that on the composition of drugs, where there will also be a discussion of the Sicyonian oil and of any other such oil. For now I am going through the simple drugs, and I shall now add the account of the other oils. For there is named also a castor oil (kikinon), produced especially in Egypt, from the fruit of the kiki, and radish-seed oil, and sesame oil, almond oil and walnut oil, and further mustard oil, mastic-tree (schinos) oil, laurel oil, melanthion (black cumin) oil, terebinth oil, mastic oil, myrtle oil, ben-nut (balanos) oil, henbane oil, and not a few others besides these, all pressed out from fruits or seeds. These differ from one another by the same differences as the fruits themselves. For castor oil is more fine-particled and more dispersing, most like old oil from the olive; hence, wherever castor oil is prescribed in some composition of a drug, if it is not available one should use the common oil, and especially if it be Sabine. Radish-seed oil is in other respects like this one, but hotter, and mustard oil hotter still than this; like the latter is the oil from melanthion. Contrary to these are myrtle oil and sesame oil, the former by being astringent, the latter because they are coarse-particled. Of mixed power are mastic-tree oil, terebinth oil and mastic oil, for they not only soften but are also astringent. Almond oil has bitterness predominating, but partakes also of some astringency; not so walnut oil, however, which is of a single, simple power, the dispersing. Hotter and more dispersing than it is laurel oil, and cedar oil more so still than this; near to the latter is the oil from liquid pitch, pine-resin oil (dadinon), less hot than laurel oil but more drying. Henbane oil is of mixed power, at once softening and cooling. Oily oil is judged by its viscosity, fine-particled oil by its translucency and purity, by the greatest extent of the body being anointed by the smallest quantity, and by its being readily drunk up by the skin. From what has been said you can now also know about the other oils, as many as are called by the same names as the perfumes—I mean rose oil, quince oil, lily oil, and all such as are made by steeping fruits or flowers or shoots or leaves in oil. For each of these, when prepared together with aromatics, is made into a perfume. More will be said about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs; having said what is useful for the present purpose, I shall take my leave. The oil will be altered according to the nature of each of the things thrown into it. For there is named also a castor oil (kikinon), produced especially in Egypt, from the fruit of the kiki, and radish-seed oil, and sesame oil, almond oil and walnut oil, and further mustard oil, mastic-tree (schinos) oil, laurel oil, melanthion (black cumin) oil, terebinth oil, mastic oil, myrtle oil, ben-nut (balanos) oil, henbane oil, and not a few others besides these, all pressed out from fruits or seeds. These differ from one another by the same differences as the fruits themselves. For castor oil is more fine-particled and more dispersing, most like old oil from the olive; hence, wherever castor oil is prescribed in some composition of a drug, if it is not available one should use the common oil, and especially if it be Sabine. Radish-seed oil is in other respects like this one, but hotter, and mustard oil hotter still than this; like the latter is the oil from melanthion. Contrary to these are myrtle oil and sesame oil, the former by being astringent, the latter because they are coarse-particled. Of mixed power are mastic-tree oil, terebinth oil and mastic oil, for they not only soften but are also astringent. Almond oil has bitterness predominating, but partakes also of some astringency; not so walnut oil, however, which is of a single, simple power, the dispersing. Hotter and more dispersing than it is laurel oil, and cedar oil more so still than this; near to the latter is the oil from liquid pitch, pine-resin oil (dadinon), less hot than laurel oil but more drying. Henbane oil is of mixed power, at once softening and cooling. Castor oil loosens the belly, and the oil from the Cnidian berry still more than this, and so much the more as its berry is more purgative than the kiki itself. The oil from the wild olive, too, is not of a simple mixture, but at once cleansing and astringent. This is the driest, as oils go, and after it the Istrian, and next to these the Spanish. The oiliest are the Libyan and the Cilician, while the Sabine is at once oily and fine-particled; in the middle of all those mentioned lies the oil of the Cycladic islands, Greece and Asia. Oily oil is judged by its viscosity, fine-particled oil by its translucency and purity, by the greatest extent of the body being anointed by the smallest quantity, and by its being readily drunk up by the skin. From what has been said you can now also know about the other oils, as many as are called by the same names as the perfumes—I mean rose oil, quince oil, lily oil, and all such as are made by steeping fruits or flowers or shoots or leaves in oil. For each of these, when prepared together with aromatics, is made into a perfume. More will be said about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs; having said what is useful for the present purpose, I shall take my leave. The oil will be altered according to the nature of each of the things thrown into it. From what you learn about each of the things thrown in, throughout this whole work in general, from these you would be able to know also about the oil of each of them individually.
